statement: Two unequal magnitudes being set out, if from the greater there be subtracted a magnitude greater than its half, and from that which is left a magnitude greater than its half, and if this process be repeated continually, there will be left some magnitude which will be less than the lesser magnitude set out.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB and C be two unequal magnitudes, with AB the greater. We must show that by repeatedly subtracting from AB a magnitude greater than its half, there will eventually remain a magnitude less than C.

**Step 2.** Since C and AB are magnitudes of the same kind, they have a ratio to one another (D5.4). Therefore, some multiple of C exceeds AB. That is, there exists a natural number such that when C is multiplied sufficiently, the result exceeds AB.

**Step 3.** By repeated doubling of C, form a sequence: let C1 = C, and let C2 = C1 + C1, and continue doubling in this manner until we obtain a magnitude DE such that DE exceeds AB. Concretely, let DE be the result of doubling C exactly k times, so that DE = 2^k times C, and DE > AB. Such a k exists by the property established in Step 2. Label the successive halves: DE is divided into DF and FE with DF = FE, and FE is divided into FG and GE with FG = GE, and so on, with the final piece at the end of this halving chain being equal to C.

**Step 4.** Now from AB subtract a magnitude greater than its half, leaving a remainder, call it AB1. Since more than half was removed, AB1 is less than half of AB.

**Step 5.** Since AB < DE, half of AB is less than half of DE, that is, less than DF. Therefore AB1, being less than half of AB, is certainly less than DF = (1/2)DE. But DF = FE, so AB1 < FE. In other words, after one subtraction from AB, the remainder AB1 is less than DE after one halving (which equals FE). This follows because the whole is greater than the part (CN5): AB is less than DE, so any quantity less than half of AB is less than half of DE.

**Step 6.** From AB1 subtract a magnitude greater than its half, leaving a remainder AB2. By the same reasoning as in Step 5, since AB1 < FE, we get AB2 < half of FE. But half of FE is the next piece in the halving chain of DE.

**Step 7.** Continue this process. At each stage, the remainder of the AB-sequence is less than the corresponding piece in the halving chain of DE. After k such subtractions, the AB-remainder is less than the final piece of the halving chain of DE, which by construction in Step 3 equals C.

**Step 8.** Therefore, after a finite number of subtractions of more than half, the remainder of AB is less than C. This is what was to be proved.

statement: If, when the less of two unequal magnitudes is continually subtracted in turn from the greater, that which is left never measures the one before it, the magnitudes will be incommensurable.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let A and B be two unequal magnitudes, with A greater than B, such that when the less is continually subtracted in turn from the greater, the remainder never measures the magnitude before it. We must show that A and B are incommensurable.

**Step 2.** Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that A and B are commensurable. Then by Definition D10.1.1, there exists some magnitude C that measures both A and B.

**Step 3.** Since C measures B, and B can be subtracted from A repeatedly, C also measures the remainder when B is subtracted from A as many times as possible. For if C measures two magnitudes, it measures the less subtracted from the greater: when B is subtracted from A, the remainder R1 satisfies A = nB + R1 where R1 < B. Since C measures A and C measures nB (because C measures B), by Common Notion CN3 (if equals be subtracted from equals, the remainders are equal), C measures R1.

**Step 4.** Likewise, since C measures B and C measures R1, when R1 is subtracted from B as many times as possible to obtain remainder R2, the same reasoning shows C measures R2. At each stage of the anthyphairesis, the common measure C measures both the current magnitude and the remainder.

**Step 5.** Now, C is a fixed positive magnitude, and the successive remainders R1, R2, R3, ... form a decreasing sequence of positive magnitudes (each remainder is less than the preceding subtrahend). By Proposition 10.1, if from a magnitude we continually subtract more than half (and in fact subtracting the remainder at least once is subtracting at least as much as half, since the remainder is less than the subtrahend), we eventually reach a magnitude less than any given magnitude. In particular, the remainders must eventually become less than C.

**Step 6.** But C measures every remainder in the sequence, so every remainder is at least as large as C (since if C measures a magnitude, that magnitude is a multiple of C and hence no smaller than C, by Definition D5.1). This contradicts the conclusion of Step 5 that a remainder smaller than C must eventually appear.

**Step 7.** Therefore our assumption that A and B are commensurable is false. Hence A and B are incommensurable, which is what was to be proved.

statement: Given two commensurable magnitudes, to find their greatest common measure.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let A and B be two given commensurable magnitudes, and let A be the greater (if they are equal, then B itself measures A, and B is the greatest common measure; so assume A is greater than B). We are to find their greatest common measure. [D10.1.1]

**Step 2.** Since A and B are commensurable, by definition there exists some magnitude C that measures both A and B. [D10.1.1]

**Step 3.** Now perform the process of repeated subtraction (antanairesis): subtract the less, B, from the greater, A, repeatedly. If B measures A, then B is a common measure of A and B. Since B measures itself, and B measures A, B is a common measure. Moreover, since every common measure of A and B must measure B, and B is no greater than itself, B is the greatest common measure. In this case we are done.

**Step 4.** If B does not measure A, then after repeatedly subtracting B from A, some magnitude less than B is left; call this remainder R1 (where R1 = A - nB for the largest n such that nB < A, and R1 < B). [CN5, D5.1]

**Step 5.** If R1 measures B, then R1 is the greatest common measure (as will be shown below). If R1 does not measure B, subtract R1 from B repeatedly, leaving some remainder R2 with R2 < R1. Continue this process.

**Step 6.** We claim this process must terminate. For suppose it does not terminate, so that the less is never measured by the remainder. Then by Proposition 10.2, A and B would be incommensurable. But A and B are given as commensurable, a contradiction. Therefore the process must terminate; that is, at some stage a remainder exactly measures the one before it. [10.2]

**Step 7.** Let the process terminate with the last nonzero remainder being E, so that E exactly measures the remainder before it. We shall show E is the greatest common measure of A and B.

**Step 8.** First, we show E is a common measure of A and B. Since E measures the previous remainder, and the previous remainder together with multiples of E reconstitutes the remainder before that, E also measures that earlier remainder. Continuing to unwind the chain of subtractions: at each stage, the magnitude being subtracted from is equal to a multiple of the subtracted magnitude plus the next remainder, so if E measures both the subtracted magnitude and the remainder, then E measures the magnitude being subtracted from. [D5.1, D5.2, CN2]

**Step 9.** Unwinding completely: E measures the last two remainders, hence it measures the one before them, and so on, until we conclude E measures B, and since E measures B and the first remainder R1, it measures A (because A equals a multiple of B plus R1). Therefore E is a common measure of A and B.

**Step 10.** Now we show E is the greatest common measure. Let F be any common measure of A and B. Since F measures A and F measures B, F measures the remainder R1 = A - nB (because if F measures both A and nB, then F measures their difference). [CN3]

**Step 11.** Similarly, since F measures B and F measures R1, F measures the next remainder R2 = B - mR1. Continuing down the chain of remainders, F measures every successive remainder, and in particular F measures E.

**Step 12.** Since F measures E, we have F is less than or equal to E. [D5.1, CN5] Therefore every common measure of A and B measures E, and hence no common measure exceeds E.

**Step 13.** Therefore E is the greatest common measure of the commensurable magnitudes A and B. Q.E.F.

statement: Given three commensurable magnitudes, to find their greatest common measure.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let A, B, C be three commensurable magnitudes. We seek their greatest common measure.

**Step 2.** Since A, B, C are commensurable, by definition (D10.1.1) there exists a magnitude that measures all three. In particular, A and B are commensurable.

**Step 3.** Since A and B are commensurable, by Proposition 10.3 we can find their greatest common measure. Let D be the greatest common measure of A and B. Then D measures A and D measures B, and any common measure of A and B also measures D.

**Step 4.** We now show that D and C are commensurable. Since A, B, C are commensurable, there exists some common measure G that measures each of A, B, and C (D10.1.1). Since G measures both A and B, G is a common measure of A and B, so by 10.3, G measures D. Since G measures both D and C, D and C are commensurable (D10.1.1).

**Step 5.** Since D and C are commensurable, by Proposition 10.3 we can find their greatest common measure. Let E be the greatest common measure of D and C. Then E measures D and E measures C, and any common measure of D and C also measures E.

**Step 6.** We show that E is a common measure of A, B, and C. Since E measures D and D measures A, E measures A. Since E measures D and D measures B, E measures B. And E measures C directly from Step 5. Therefore E is a common measure of A, B, and C.

**Step 7.** We show that E is the greatest common measure. Let F be any common measure of A, B, and C. Since F measures both A and B, F is a common measure of A and B, so by 10.3, F measures D (the greatest common measure of A and B). Since F also measures C, F is a common measure of D and C, so by 10.3, F measures E (the greatest common measure of D and C). Since every common measure of A, B, C measures E, E is the greatest common measure of A, B, and C.

**Step 8.** Therefore, given three commensurable magnitudes A, B, C, their greatest common measure E has been found. Q.E.F.

statement: Commensurable magnitudes have to one another the ratio which a number has to a number.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let A and B be commensurable magnitudes. By D10.1.1, there exists a magnitude C which measures both A and B.

**Step 2.** Since C measures A, by D5.1 and D5.2, A is a multiple of C. Let A be the m-th multiple of C, that is, A = mC, where m is a number (D7.2). Similarly, since C measures B, let B be the n-th multiple of C, that is, B = nC, where n is a number.

**Step 3.** We must show that A : B :: m : n. By D5.5, this requires that for any positive integers s and t: if s*m > t*n then sA > tB; if s*m = t*n then sA = tB; and if s*m < t*n then sA < tB.

**Step 4.** Since A = mC (that is, A is the m-th multiple of C), by 5.3 the s-th equimultiple of A equals the (s*m)-th multiple of C, so sA = (sm)C. Similarly, since B = nC, the t-th equimultiple of B equals the (t*n)-th multiple of C, so tB = (tn)C.

**Step 5.** Suppose sm > tn. Then sm = tn + r for some positive remainder r. Hence (sm)C = (tn)C + rC, and by CN5 the whole (sm)C is greater than the part (tn)C. Therefore sA > tB.

**Step 6.** Suppose sm = tn. Then (sm)C and (tn)C are the same multiple of C, so sA = tB.

**Step 7.** Suppose sm < tn. By the same reasoning as Step 5 (with roles exchanged), (tn)C > (sm)C, so tB > sA, that is, sA < tB.

**Step 8.** Since for every pair of positive integers s and t, the multiples sA and tB compare in the same way as the numbers sm and tn respectively, by D5.5 the ratio A : B is the same as the ratio m : n.

**Step 9.** Since m and n are numbers (D7.2), A and B have to one another the ratio which a number has to a number. Q.E.D.

statement: If two magnitudes have to one another the ratio which a number has to a number, the magnitudes will be commensurable.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let A and B be two magnitudes such that A : B = D : E, where D and E are numbers. We wish to show that A and B are commensurable.

**Step 2.** Since D is a number, divide the magnitude A into D equal parts, and let C be one of those equal parts. Then A is the D-fold multiple of C, that is, A = D · C [D5.2].

**Step 3.** Since A : B = D : E (given) and A = D · C (Step 2), we have D · C : B = D : E.

**Step 4.** Now consider the magnitude E · C. We claim that D · C : E · C = D : E. To see this, take any positive integers p and q. Then p · (D · C) = (pD) · C and q · (E · C) = (qE) · C. Since C is a magnitude greater than zero, (pD) · C is greater than, equal to, or less than (qE) · C according as pD is greater than, equal to, or less than qE. But this is precisely the condition for the number ratio D : E [D7.20]. Therefore, by the definition of same ratio [D5.5], the magnitude ratio D · C : E · C equals the number ratio D : E.

**Step 5.** From Step 3 we have D · C : B = D : E, and from Step 4 we have D · C : E · C = D : E. Since both ratios are the same as D : E, by Proposition 5.11, D · C : B = D · C : E · C.

**Step 6.** Since the same magnitude D · C has the same ratio to both B and E · C, by the second part of Proposition 5.9, B = E · C.

**Step 7.** Since A = D · C (Step 2) and B = E · C (Step 6), the magnitude C measures both A and B [D5.1, D5.2]. Therefore, A and B have a common measure, and by definition they are commensurable [D10.1.1]. Q.E.D.

statement: Incommensurable magnitudes have not to one another the ratio which a number has to a number.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let A and B be incommensurable magnitudes. We are to prove that A does not have to B the ratio which a number has to a number.

**Step 2.** Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that A has to B the ratio which some number C has to some number D; that is, suppose A:B = C:D.

**Step 3.** Since A and B are magnitudes such that A:B equals the ratio of number C to number D, by Proposition 10.6 (if two magnitudes have to one another the ratio which a number has to a number, the magnitudes will be commensurable), A and B are commensurable.

**Step 4.** But A and B are incommensurable by hypothesis (D10.1.1: magnitudes are incommensurable which cannot have any common measure). This is a contradiction.

**Step 5.** Therefore the supposition is false, and incommensurable magnitudes have not to one another the ratio which a number has to a number. Q.E.D.

statement: If two magnitudes have not to one another the ratio which a number has to a number, the magnitudes will be incommensurable.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let A and B be two magnitudes which have not to one another the ratio which a number has to a number. We claim that A and B are incommensurable.

**Step 2.** Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that A and B are commensurable, that is, that there exists some magnitude C which measures both A and B [D10.1.1].

**Step 3.** Since A and B are commensurable, by Proposition 10.5, A and B have to one another the ratio which a number has to a number [10.5].

**Step 4.** But this contradicts the hypothesis that A and B have not to one another the ratio which a number has to a number.

**Step 5.** Therefore the assumption that A and B are commensurable is false. Hence A and B are incommensurable [D10.1.1].

Q.E.D.

statement: The squares on straight lines commensurable in length have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number; and squares which have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number will also have their sides commensurable in length. But the squares on straight lines incommensurable in length have not to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number; and squares which have not to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number will not have their sides commensurable in length either.
proof:
**Step 1.** The proposition has four parts. We prove each in turn.

PART I: The squares on straight lines commensurable in length have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number.

**Step 2.** Let A and B be straight lines commensurable in length. Since A and B are commensurable, by 10.5, A has to B the ratio which a number has to a number. Let A:B = m:n, where m and n are numbers.

**Step 3.** By 6.20, since squares are similar rectilineal figures, the square on A has to the square on B the duplicate ratio of that which A has to B. That is, sq(A):sq(B) is the duplicate ratio of A:B.

**Step 4.** Since A:B = m:n, the duplicate ratio of A:B is the duplicate ratio of m:n. By 8.11, between two square numbers there is one mean proportional number, and the square has to the square the duplicate ratio of that which the side has to the side. Therefore m^2:n^2 is the duplicate ratio of m:n.

**Step 5.** Since the duplicate ratio of A:B equals the duplicate ratio of m:n, and sq(A):sq(B) is the duplicate ratio of A:B, we have sq(A):sq(B) = m^2:n^2. Now m^2 is a square number and n^2 is a square number (D7.18). Therefore the squares on A and B have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number.

PART II: Squares which have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number will also have their sides commensurable in length.

**Step 6.** Conversely, let the square on A have to the square on B the ratio which a square number has to a square number. That is, let sq(A):sq(B) = p^2:q^2, where p and q are numbers so that p^2 and q^2 are square numbers.

**Step 7.** By 6.20, sq(A):sq(B) is the duplicate ratio of A:B. By 8.11, p^2:q^2 is the duplicate ratio of p:q.

**Step 8.** Since sq(A):sq(B) = p^2:q^2, the duplicate ratio of A:B equals the duplicate ratio of p:q. Therefore A:B = p:q. Since p and q are numbers, A has to B the ratio which a number has to a number.

**Step 9.** By 10.6, since A and B have to one another the ratio which a number has to a number, A and B are commensurable in length.

PART III: The squares on straight lines incommensurable in length have not to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number.

**Step 10.** Let A and B be straight lines incommensurable in length. Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that sq(A):sq(B) equals a square number to a square number. Then by Part II (Steps 6-9), A and B would be commensurable in length. But this contradicts the hypothesis that A and B are incommensurable in length. Therefore sq(A):sq(B) does not have the ratio which a square number has to a square number.

PART IV: Squares which have not to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number will not have their sides commensurable in length either.

**Step 11.** Let sq(A):sq(B) not have the ratio which a square number has to a square number. Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that A and B are commensurable in length. Then by Part I (Steps 2-5), sq(A):sq(B) would have the ratio which a square number has to a square number. But this contradicts the hypothesis. Therefore A and B are not commensurable in length, that is, they are incommensurable in length.

**Step 12.** Therefore the squares on straight lines commensurable in length have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number, and squares which have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number will also have their sides commensurable in length; and the squares on straight lines incommensurable in length have not to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number, and squares which have not to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number will not have their sides commensurable in length either. Q.E.D.

statement: To find two straight lines incommensurable, the one in length only, and the other in square also, with an assigned straight line.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let A be the assigned straight line. We are required to find two straight lines, one incommensurable with A in length only, and the other incommensurable with A in square also.

**Step 2.** Construct a straight line B such that the square on B is equal to twice the square on A. This can be done by setting up a right angle and making each of the two sides containing the right angle equal to A; the hypotenuse, by the Pythagorean theorem [1.47], has its square equal to the sum of the squares on the two sides, that is, equal to twice the square on A. Let B be this hypotenuse.

**Step 3.** Then the square on B has to the square on A the ratio 2 : 1, which is the ratio of a number to a number. Therefore the square on B is commensurable with the square on A [10.6].

**Step 4.** Now 2 is not a square number, and 1 is a square number, so the ratio 2 : 1 is not the ratio of a square number to a square number. Therefore, by 10.9, B is incommensurable in length with A.

**Step 5.** Since B is incommensurable in length with A, yet the square on B is commensurable with the square on A, B is incommensurable with A in length only [D10.1.1, D10.1.2]. This is the first required line.

**Step 6.** Next, take A and B, and find their mean proportional C, so that A is to C as C is to B [6.13].

**Step 7.** Then the square on C is equal to the rectangle contained by A and B, that is, A : C :: C : B implies the square on C equals the rectangle A by B [6.17].

**Step 8.** Since B is incommensurable in length with A, the ratio of B to A is not the ratio of a number to a number [10.7].

**Step 9.** Now the square on C is to the square on A as B is to A. For since the square on C equals the rectangle A by B, we have the square on C to the square on A equal to (A times B) to (A times A), which equals B to A [6.1].

**Step 10.** Since the ratio of B to A is not the ratio of a number to a number [Step 8], the ratio of the square on C to the square on A is not the ratio of a number to a number either.

**Step 11.** Therefore, by 10.8, the square on C is incommensurable with the square on A, which means C is incommensurable in square with A [D10.1.2]. This is the second required line.

**Step 12.** Therefore we have found B, incommensurable with the assigned straight line A in length only, and C, incommensurable with A in square also, which is what was required to find. Q.E.F.

statement: If four magnitudes be proportional, and the first be commensurable with the second, the third will also be commensurable with the fourth; and, if the first be incommensurable with the second, the third will also be incommensurable with the fourth.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let A, B, C, D be four magnitudes such that A : B :: C : D [D5.5, D5.6].

**Step 2.** First, suppose that A is commensurable with B [D10.1.1].

**Step 3.** Since A is commensurable with B, by Proposition 10.5, A has to B the ratio which a number has to a number. That is, there exist numbers m and n such that A : B :: m : n [10.5].

**Step 4.** But A : B :: C : D (given). Therefore C : D :: m : n, since ratios that are the same as the same ratio are the same as one another [D5.5, D5.6].

**Step 5.** Since C has to D the ratio which the number m has to the number n, by Proposition 10.6, C is commensurable with D [10.6].

**Step 6.** Next, suppose that A is incommensurable with B [D10.1.1].

**Step 7.** Since A is incommensurable with B, by Proposition 10.7, A does not have to B the ratio which a number has to a number [10.7].

**Step 8.** But A : B :: C : D (given). Therefore C does not have to D the ratio which a number has to a number either. For if C did have to D the ratio of a number to a number, say C : D :: p : q for some numbers p and q, then since A : B :: C : D, we would have A : B :: p : q, meaning A would have to B the ratio of a number to a number, contradicting Step 7 [D5.5, D5.6].

**Step 9.** Since C does not have to D the ratio which a number has to a number, by Proposition 10.8, C is incommensurable with D [10.8].

**Step 10.** Therefore, if four magnitudes be proportional, and the first be commensurable with the second, the third will also be commensurable with the fourth; and if the first be incommensurable with the second, the third will also be incommensurable with the fourth. Q.E.D.

statement: Magnitudes commensurable with the same magnitude are commensurable with one another also.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let A and B each be commensurable with a magnitude C. We are to prove that A and B are commensurable with one another.

**Step 2.** Since A is commensurable with C, by Proposition 10.5, A has to C the ratio which a number has to a number. Let A:C :: m:n, where m and n are numbers.

**Step 3.** Since B is commensurable with C, by Proposition 10.5, B has to C the ratio which a number has to a number. Let B:C :: p:q, where p and q are numbers.

**Step 4.** Since p multiplies the two numbers m and n, by Proposition 7.17, the products pm and pn have to one another the ratio which m has to n. That is, pm:pn :: m:n.

**Step 5.** But A:C :: m:n (Step 2) and m:n :: pm:pn (Step 4). Therefore, by Proposition 5.11, A:C :: pm:pn.

**Step 6.** Since n multiplies the two numbers p and q, by Proposition 7.17, the products np and nq have to one another the ratio which p has to q. That is, np:nq :: p:q.

**Step 7.** But B:C :: p:q (Step 3) and p:q :: np:nq (Step 6). Therefore, by Proposition 5.11, B:C :: np:nq. By the definition of inverse ratio (D5.13), C:B :: nq:np.

**Step 8.** We now have A:C :: pm:np and C:B :: np:nq, where pm, np, and nq are all numbers. By Proposition 5.22 (ex aequali), A:B :: pm:nq.

**Step 9.** Since m, n, p, and q are numbers, pm and nq are also numbers (being products of numbers). Therefore A has to B the ratio which a number has to a number.

**Step 10.** Since A has to B the ratio which a number has to a number, by Proposition 10.6, A is commensurable with B.

**Step 11.** Therefore, magnitudes commensurable with the same magnitude are commensurable with one another also. Q.E.D.

statement: If two magnitudes be commensurable, and the one of them be incommensurable with any magnitude, the remaining one will also be incommensurable with the same.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let A and B be two commensurable magnitudes, and let A be incommensurable with some magnitude C. We are to prove that B is also incommensurable with C. [D10.1.1]

**Step 2.** Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that B is commensurable with C. [D10.1.1]

**Step 3.** Since A is commensurable with B (given), and B is commensurable with C (assumption), then by Proposition 10.12, magnitudes commensurable with the same magnitude are commensurable with one another. Here A is commensurable with B, and C is commensurable with B, so A is commensurable with C. [10.12]

**Step 4.** But A was given as incommensurable with C. This is a contradiction. [D10.1.1]

**Step 5.** Therefore the assumption that B is commensurable with C is false, and B is incommensurable with C. [D10.1.1]

**Step 6.** Therefore, if two magnitudes be commensurable, and one of them be incommensurable with any magnitude, the remaining one will also be incommensurable with the same. Q.E.D.

statement: If four straight lines be proportional, and the square on the first be greater than the square on the second by the square on a straight line commensurable with the first, the square on the third will also be greater than the square on the fourth by  the square on a straight line commensurable with the third. And, if the square on the first be greater than the square on the second by the square on a straight line incommensurable with the first, the square on the third will also be greater than the square on the fourth by the square on a straight line in-commensurable with the third.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let A, B, C, D be four straight lines such that A:B :: C:D. Suppose that sq(A) is greater than sq(B) by the square on a straight line commensurable with A; that is, let E be a straight line such that sq(A) = sq(B) + sq(E), where E is commensurable in length with A.

**Step 2.** Since A:B :: C:D, and squares are similar rectilineal figures similarly described on these lines, by 6.22 we have sq(A):sq(B) :: sq(C):sq(D).

**Step 3.** Since sq(A) > sq(B) and sq(A):sq(B) :: sq(C):sq(D), by 5.14 we have sq(C) > sq(D). Let F be the straight line such that sq(C) = sq(D) + sq(F); such a line exists by 1.47 applied to a right triangle with hypotenuse C and one leg D.

**Step 4.** Since sq(A) = sq(B) + sq(E), we may write the proportion from Step 2 as (sq(B) + sq(E)):sq(B) :: (sq(D) + sq(F)):sq(D). Applying 5.17 (separando), we obtain sq(E):sq(B) :: sq(F):sq(D).

**Step 5.** Since sq(E):sq(B) :: sq(F):sq(D), and these are similar rectilineal figures (squares) similarly described on the lines E, B and F, D respectively, by the converse part of 6.22, we conclude that E:B :: F:D.

**Step 6.** From the original proportion A:B :: C:D, by 5.16 (alternando) we have A:C :: B:D. From E:B :: F:D (Step 5), by 5.16 (alternando) we have E:F :: B:D. Therefore A:C :: E:F, since both equal B:D [CN1].

**Step 7.** From A:C :: E:F, by 5.16 (alternando) again, we obtain A:E :: C:F.

**Step 8.** Now E is commensurable in length with A (given). Since A:E :: C:F and A is commensurable with E, by 10.11 (if four magnitudes be proportional and the first be commensurable with the second, the third will also be commensurable with the fourth), C is commensurable in length with F. Therefore the square on the third C is greater than the square on the fourth D by the square on F, a straight line commensurable with C.

**Step 9.** For the second part, suppose instead that E is incommensurable in length with A, where again sq(A) = sq(B) + sq(E). By the identical argument of Steps 2 through 7, we still obtain A:E :: C:F, where sq(C) = sq(D) + sq(F). Since A is incommensurable with E, by 10.11 (if the first be incommensurable with the second, the third will also be incommensurable with the fourth), C is incommensurable in length with F. Therefore the square on the third C is greater than the square on the fourth D by the square on F, a straight line incommensurable with C.

**Step 10.** Thus in both cases the commensurability or incommensurability relation between the excess-line and the first term is transferred to the corresponding excess-line and the third term. Q.E.D.

statement: If two commensurable magnitudes be added together, the whole will also be commensurable with each of them; and, if the whole be commensurable with one of them, the original magnitudes will also be commensurable.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let A and B be two commensurable magnitudes. We are to prove first that A+B is commensurable with each of A and B, and second that if A+B is commensurable with one of them (say A), then A and B are commensurable with one another.

**Step 2.** [Part I] Since A and B are commensurable, by definition (D10.1.1) there exists some magnitude C which measures both A and B. Since C measures A, A is a multiple of C (D5.2), so A = pC for some number p. Since C measures B, B is a multiple of C (D5.2), so B = qC for some number q.

**Step 3.** Then A + B = pC + qC = (p + q)C, since combining p copies of C with q copies of C yields (p + q) copies of C (CN2). Since p and q are numbers, (p + q) is also a number, and therefore C measures A + B.

**Step 4.** Since C measures both A + B and A, the magnitudes A + B and A are measured by the same measure C, so A + B is commensurable with A (D10.1.1). Since C measures both A + B and B, the magnitudes A + B and B are measured by the same measure C, so A + B is commensurable with B (D10.1.1). This completes Part I.

**Step 5.** [Part II] Now suppose conversely that the whole A + B is commensurable with one of the summands, say A. We are to prove that A and B are commensurable.

**Step 6.** Since A + B is commensurable with A (D10.1.1), there exists a magnitude C which measures both A + B and A. Since C measures A + B, we have A + B = mC for some number m (D5.2). Since C measures A, we have A = nC for some number n (D5.2).

**Step 7.** Now A + B is greater than A, since B is a magnitude and the whole is greater than the part (CN5). Therefore mC is greater than nC, so m is greater than n.

**Step 8.** Since A + B = mC and A = nC, subtracting equals from equals (CN3) gives B = (A + B) - A = mC - nC = (m - n)C. Since m is greater than n, (m - n) is a number, and therefore C measures B.

**Step 9.** Since C measures both A and B, the magnitudes A and B are measured by the same measure C, so A and B are commensurable (D10.1.1).

**Step 10.** Therefore, if two commensurable magnitudes be added together, the whole is commensurable with each of them; and if the whole be commensurable with one of them, the original magnitudes are also commensurable. Q.E.D.

statement: If two incommensurable magnitudes be added together, the whole will also be incommensurable with each of them; and, if the whole be incommensurable with one of them, the original magnitudes will also be incommensurable.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB and BC be two magnitudes, and let AC be their sum, so that AC = AB + BC.

**Step 2.** (Part I) Suppose AB and BC are incommensurable [D10.1.1]. We claim AC is incommensurable with each of AB and BC.

**Step 3.** Assume for the sake of contradiction that AC is commensurable with AB. Since AC = AB + BC and AC is commensurable with AB, by Proposition 10.15 (if the whole be commensurable with one of the summands, the original magnitudes are also commensurable), AB and BC are commensurable. But this contradicts the hypothesis that AB and BC are incommensurable. Therefore AC is incommensurable with AB.

**Step 4.** By the same argument, assume for contradiction that AC is commensurable with BC. Then by 10.15, since AC = AB + BC and AC is commensurable with BC, the magnitudes AB and BC are commensurable, again contradicting the hypothesis. Therefore AC is incommensurable with BC.

**Step 5.** Hence, if AB and BC are incommensurable, AC is incommensurable with each of AB and BC.

**Step 6.** (Part II) Now suppose conversely that AC is incommensurable with one of the summands, say AB. We claim AB and BC are incommensurable.

**Step 7.** Assume for contradiction that AB and BC are commensurable. Then by 10.15 (if two commensurable magnitudes be added together, the whole is commensurable with each of them), AC is commensurable with AB. But this contradicts the hypothesis that AC is incommensurable with AB. Therefore AB and BC are incommensurable.

**Step 8.** Therefore, if two incommensurable magnitudes be added together, the whole is incommensurable with each of them; and if the whole be incommensurable with one of them, the original magnitudes are also incommensurable. Q.E.D.

statement: If there be two unequal straight lines, and to the greater there be applied a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on the less and deficient by a square figure, and if it divide it into parts which are commensurable in length, then the square on the greater will be greater than the square on the less by the square on a straight line commensurable with the greater. And, if the square on the greater be greater than the square on the less by the square on a straight line commensurable with  the greater, and if there be applied to the greater a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on the less and deficient by a square figure, it will divide it into parts which are commensurable in length.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let A and B be two unequal straight lines with A greater than B. To A let there be applied a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on B and deficient by a square figure. This is possible by 6.28, since the fourth part of the square on B does not exceed the square on half of A (for A is greater than B). Let this application divide A into parts; call them the segments x and y, so that A equals x together with y, and the rectangle contained by x and y equals the fourth part of the square on B.

**Step 2.** Since A is divided into x and y, by 2.5 the rectangle contained by x and y together with the square on half the difference of x and y equals the square on half of A. That is, rect(x, y) + sq((x - y)/2) = sq(A/2).

**Step 3.** But rect(x, y) equals the fourth part of sq(B), that is, sq(B/2). Therefore sq(A/2) - sq(B/2) = sq((x - y)/2), by CN3.

**Step 4.** Multiplying throughout by four (i.e., since each of these squares is the fourth part of the corresponding larger square, by 6.22 and 6.1), we obtain sq(A) - sq(B) = sq(x - y). Thus the square on A is greater than the square on B by the square on the straight line x - y.

**Step 5.** (Forward direction.) Suppose x and y are commensurable in length. Since A equals x together with y, by 10.15 the whole A is commensurable with each of x and y. Now x and y are commensurable, so their difference x - y is also commensurable with their sum A, by 10.15 (for if x and y are commensurable, then x - y and x + y are each commensurable with x and with y, and hence with one another through 10.12). Therefore x - y is commensurable with A. But from Step 4, sq(A) - sq(B) = sq(x - y), so the square on A is greater than the square on B by the square on a straight line commensurable with A.

**Step 6.** (Converse direction.) Suppose the square on A is greater than the square on B by the square on a straight line commensurable with A. From Step 4, sq(A) - sq(B) = sq(x - y), so the straight line by which the square on A exceeds the square on B is x - y. Therefore x - y is commensurable with A.

**Step 7.** But A equals x + y. Now since x - y is commensurable with x + y, by 10.15 the sum (x + y) together with the difference (x - y) yields: twice x equals (x + y) + (x - y), and twice y equals (x + y) - (x - y). Since x + y and x - y are commensurable, their sum 2x and their difference 2y are commensurable by 10.15 and CN2 and CN3. Hence x and y are commensurable (for magnitudes that are doubles of commensurable magnitudes are themselves commensurable, by 10.6 and 10.5, since commensurable magnitudes have to one another the ratio of a number to a number, and halving preserves this).

**Step 8.** Therefore the parallelogram applied to A, equal to the fourth part of the square on B and deficient by a square figure, divides A into parts which are commensurable in length. Q.E.D.

statement: If there be two unequal straight lines, and to the greater there be applied a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on the less and deficient by a square figure, and if it divide it into parts which are incommensurable, the square on the greater will be greater than the square on the less by the square on a straight line incommensurable with the greater. And, if the square on the greater be greater than the square on the less by the square on a straight line incommensurable with the greater, and if there be applied to the greater a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on the less and deficient by a square figure, it divides it into parts which are incommensurable. Let A, BC be two unequal straight lines, of which BC is the greater, and to BC let there be applied a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on the less, A, and deficient by a square figure.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let A and BC be two unequal straight lines with BC the greater. To BC let there be applied a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on A and deficient by a square figure. Let this application divide BC into BD and DC, so that the rectangle BD by DC equals one-fourth of the square on A.

**Step 2.** Bisect BC at E [1.10], so that BE = EC = (1/2)BC.

**Step 3.** Since BC is bisected at E and divided unequally at D, by 2.5 the rectangle BD by DC together with the square on ED equals the square on EC, that is, the square on BE. Therefore sq(BE) = rect(BD, DC) + sq(ED).

**Step 4.** Since rect(BD, DC) = (1/4)sq(A) by construction, we have sq(BE) - (1/4)sq(A) = sq(ED), whence 4 sq(BE) - sq(A) = 4 sq(ED) [CN2, CN3]. But 4 sq(BE) = sq(BC) (since BE = (1/2)BC). Therefore sq(BC) - sq(A) = sq(2 ED), and the straight line by which the square on BC exceeds the square on A in square is equal to twice ED.

**Part I (Forward direction).** Suppose BD and DC are incommensurable.

**Step 5.** Since BD and DC are incommensurable and BD + DC = BC, by 10.16 (forward part) BC is incommensurable with each of BD and DC. In particular, BC is incommensurable with BD.

**Step 6.** Now BC = 2 BE, so BC and BE have the ratio 2 to 1, which is a ratio of number to number. Therefore BC and BE are commensurable [10.6].

**Step 7.** Since BC is commensurable with BE (Step 6) and BC is incommensurable with BD (Step 5), by 10.13 BE is incommensurable with BD.

**Step 8.** Since BD = BE + ED and BD is incommensurable with BE (Step 7), by the converse part of 10.16 the magnitudes BE and ED are incommensurable.

**Step 9.** Now ED and BE are in the same ratio as 2 ED and 2 BE respectively [5.15]. Since ED is incommensurable with BE, by 10.11 the magnitude 2 ED is incommensurable with 2 BE, that is, 2 ED is incommensurable with BC.

**Step 10.** But the square on BC exceeds the square on A by the square on 2 ED (Step 4). Therefore the square on BC is greater than the square on A by the square on a straight line incommensurable with BC.

**Part II (Converse direction).** Suppose the square on BC is greater than the square on A by the square on a straight line incommensurable with BC.

**Step 11.** By Step 4, the straight line whose square equals sq(BC) - sq(A) is 2 ED. So 2 ED is incommensurable with BC by hypothesis.

**Step 12.** Since BC = 2 BE, the magnitudes 2 ED and 2 BE are incommensurable (Step 11). Now 2 ED is to 2 BE as ED is to BE [5.15]. Therefore by 10.11, ED is incommensurable with BE.

**Step 13.** Since BE + ED = BD and BE is incommensurable with ED (Step 12), by 10.16 (forward part) the whole BD is incommensurable with BE.

**Step 14.** Since BC is commensurable with BE (Step 6, which holds in both directions) and BD is incommensurable with BE (Step 13), by 10.13 BD is incommensurable with BC.

**Step 15.** Since BD + DC = BC and BD is incommensurable with BC (Step 14), by the converse part of 10.16 the magnitudes BD and DC are incommensurable.

**Step 16.** Therefore the application divides BC into parts BD and DC which are incommensurable. Q.E.D.

statement: The rectangle contained by rational straight lines commensurable in length is rational.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let A and B be rational straight lines commensurable in length with one another. Let C be the assigned rational straight line. We are to show that the rectangle contained by A and B is rational.

**Step 2.** Since A is rational, by Definition D10.1.3, A is commensurable with C either in length and in square, or in square only. In either case, the square on A is commensurable with the square on C. Therefore, by Definition D10.1.4, the square on A is rational.

**Step 3.** Since A and B are commensurable in length, by Proposition 10.5, A has to B the ratio which a number has to a number.

**Step 4.** Consider the rectangle contained by A and B, and the square on A. By Proposition 6.1, parallelograms (and rectangles) under the same height are to one another as their bases. Taking the rectangles with common side A, the rectangle contained by A and B is to the square on A (i.e., the rectangle contained by A and A) as B is to A.

**Step 5.** Since A and B are commensurable in length, B has to A the ratio which a number has to a number, by Proposition 10.5. Therefore, by Step 4, the rectangle contained by A and B has to the square on A the ratio which a number has to a number.

**Step 6.** Since the rectangle contained by A and B has to the square on A the ratio which a number has to a number, by Proposition 10.6, the rectangle contained by A and B is commensurable with the square on A.

**Step 7.** But the square on A is rational (Step 2), that is, the square on A is commensurable with the square on C. And the rectangle contained by A and B is commensurable with the square on A (Step 6). Therefore, by Proposition 10.12, the rectangle contained by A and B is commensurable with the square on C.

**Step 8.** Since the rectangle contained by A and B is commensurable with the square on the assigned rational straight line C, by Definition D10.1.4, the rectangle contained by A and B is rational. Q.E.D.

statement: If a rational area be applied to a rational straight line, it produces as breadth a straight line rational and commensurable in length with the straight line to which it is applied.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let the rational area S be applied to the rational straight line A, producing the straight line B as breadth. Then the rectangle contained by A and B equals S.

**Step 2.** Since A is a rational straight line, by D10.1.3, A is commensurable with the assigned rational straight line, whether in length and in square or in square only. In either case, A is commensurable in square with the assigned rational straight line, so the square on A is commensurable with the square on the assigned rational straight line [D10.1.2].

**Step 3.** Since S is a rational area, by D10.1.4, S is commensurable with the square on the assigned rational straight line.

**Step 4.** Since the square on A is commensurable with the square on the assigned rational straight line (Step 2), and S is also commensurable with the square on the assigned rational straight line (Step 3), it follows by 10.12 that S is commensurable with the square on A.

**Step 5.** Now the rectangle contained by A and B equals S, and the square on A is the rectangle contained by A and A. These are parallelograms of the same height A. By 6.1, parallelograms under the same height are to one another as their bases. Therefore S is to the square on A as B is to A.

**Step 6.** Since S is commensurable with the square on A (Step 4), S has to the square on A the ratio which a number has to a number [10.5]. Therefore B has to A the ratio which a number has to a number (Step 5). By 10.6, B is commensurable in length with A.

**Step 7.** Since A is rational and B is commensurable in length with A, by D10.1.3, B is also rational.

**Step 8.** Therefore, if a rational area be applied to a rational straight line, the breadth is a straight line that is both rational and commensurable in length with the straight line to which it is applied. Q.E.D.

statement: The rectangle contained by rational straight lines commensurable in square only is irrational, and the side of the square equal to it is irrational. Let the latter be called medial.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let A and B be rational straight lines commensurable in square only. We are to show that the rectangle contained by A and B is irrational, and that the side of the square equal to it is irrational.

**Step 2.** Since A and B are rational, each is commensurable in square with the assigned rational straight line, so the squares on A and B are rational areas [D10.1.3, D10.1.4]. Since A and B are commensurable in square only, the squares sq(A) and sq(B) are commensurable with one another, but A and B are incommensurable in length [D10.1.2].

**Step 3.** Consider the rectangle rect(A, B) and the square sq(A). By Proposition 6.1, rectangles (parallelograms) with the same base and under the same height are to one another as their heights. Taking the rectangles with base A and heights A and B respectively, we obtain sq(A) : rect(A, B) = A : B [6.1].

**Step 4.** Since A and B are incommensurable in length, the ratio A : B is not a ratio of a number to a number [10.7].

**Step 5.** Therefore the ratio sq(A) : rect(A, B) is not a ratio of a number to a number either, since it equals A : B.

**Step 6.** By Proposition 10.8, since sq(A) and rect(A, B) do not have to one another the ratio which a number has to a number, they are incommensurable [10.8].

**Step 7.** Now sq(A) is rational, since A is rational and the square on a rational straight line is a rational area [D10.1.4]. Since rect(A, B) is incommensurable with the rational area sq(A), the rectangle rect(A, B) is irrational [D10.1.4].

**Step 8.** Now let us construct the side of the square equal to rect(A, B). By Proposition 6.13, take the mean proportional G between A and B, so that A : G = G : B [6.13]. Then by Proposition 6.17, the rectangle contained by the extremes A and B equals the square on the mean proportional G, that is, rect(A, B) = sq(G) [6.17].

**Step 9.** Since rect(A, B) is irrational (as proved in Step 7), the square sq(G) is irrational. Therefore G is irrational, for the side of a square equal to an irrational area is irrational [D10.1.4].

**Step 10.** Let the straight line G, the side of the square equal to the rectangle contained by rational straight lines commensurable in square only, be called medial. Q.E.D.

statement: The square on a medial straight line, if applied to a rational straight line, produces as breadth a straight line rational and incommensurable in length with that to which it is applied.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let A be a medial straight line, and let B be a rational straight line. Apply the square on A to B, producing as breadth C, so that the rectangle contained by B and C equals the square on A. We must show that C is rational and incommensurable in length with B.

**Step 2.** Since A is medial, by the definition established in 10.21, the square on A is equal to the rectangle contained by two rational straight lines that are commensurable in square only. Let these rational straight lines be E and F, so that the rectangle contained by E and F equals the square on A. The square on A is therefore an irrational area [10.21].

**Step 3.** Since the rectangle E * F equals the square on A, and the square on A equals the rectangle B * C (by construction), we have that the rectangle contained by E and F equals the rectangle contained by B and C.

**Step 4.** Since the rectangle E * F equals the rectangle B * C, it follows that E is to B as C is to F [6.16].

**Step 5.** Therefore the duplicate ratio of E to B equals the duplicate ratio of C to F, which is to say E squared is to B squared as C squared is to F squared [6.22].

**Step 6.** Now E is rational and B is rational. By definition [D10.1.3], rational straight lines are commensurable in square with the assigned rational straight line, and hence with each other in square. Therefore the square on E is commensurable with the square on B [D10.1.3, 10.12].

**Step 7.** Since the square on E is commensurable with the square on B, and the square on E is to the square on B as the square on C is to the square on F [Step 5], by 10.11 the square on C is commensurable with the square on F.

**Step 8.** Since F is rational, the square on F is commensurable with the square on the assigned rational straight line [D10.1.3]. Since the square on C is commensurable with the square on F [Step 7], and the square on F is commensurable with the square on the assigned rational line, by 10.12 the square on C is commensurable with the square on the assigned rational line. Therefore C is rational [D10.1.3].

**Step 9.** It remains to show that C is incommensurable in length with B. Since the rectangle B * C equals the square on A, we have that the rectangle B * C is to the square on B as C is to B [6.1].

**Step 10.** Now the rectangle B * C equals the square on A [Step 1], and the square on A is a medial (irrational) area [Step 2, by 10.21], while the square on B is a rational area [D10.1.4, since B is rational]. Since a medial area is irrational, the square on A is incommensurable with the square on B [D10.1.4].

**Step 11.** Therefore the ratio of the rectangle B * C to the square on B is a ratio of incommensurable magnitudes. Since this ratio equals C to B [Step 9], C is incommensurable in length with B [10.11].

**Step 12.** Therefore the square on the medial straight line A, when applied to the rational straight line B, produces as breadth C, a straight line that is rational [Step 8] and incommensurable in length with B [Step 11]. Q.E.D.

statement: A straight line commensurable with a medial straight line is medial.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let A be a medial straight line, and let B be commensurable in length with A. We are to show that B is also medial.

**Step 2.** Set out a rational straight line CD [D10.1.3].

**Step 3.** To CD apply a rectangular area equal to the square on A, producing CE as breadth, so that CD * CE = sq(A). Since A is medial, by 10.22 the breadth CE is rational and incommensurable in length with CD.

**Step 4.** To CD apply a rectangular area equal to the square on B, producing CF as breadth, so that CD * CF = sq(B).

**Step 5.** Since A and B are commensurable in length, the squares on them have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number [10.9]. Therefore sq(A) and sq(B) are commensurable [10.6].

**Step 6.** Now sq(A) = CD * CE and sq(B) = CD * CF. Since these rectangles share the same side CD, by 6.1 we have CD * CE : CD * CF = CE : CF, that is, sq(A) : sq(B) = CE : CF.

**Step 7.** Since sq(A) is commensurable with sq(B), and sq(A) : sq(B) = CE : CF, it follows that CE is commensurable with CF [10.11].

**Step 8.** Since CE is rational and CF is commensurable with CE, CF is also rational [D10.1.3, 10.12].

**Step 9.** Since CE is incommensurable in length with CD (Step 3), and CF is commensurable with CE (Step 7), it follows that CF is also incommensurable in length with CD [10.13].

**Step 10.** Therefore CD and CF are both rational straight lines commensurable in square only (they are each rational, hence commensurable in square with the assigned rational line and therefore with each other, yet incommensurable in length with each other). By 10.21, the rectangle CD * CF is irrational, and the side of the square equal to it is medial.

**Step 11.** But CD * CF = sq(B), so B is the side of a square equal to the rectangle contained by the rational straight lines CD and CF which are commensurable in square only. Therefore B is medial [10.21]. Q.E.D.

statement: The rectangle contained by medial straight lines commensurable in length is medial.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let A and B be medial straight lines commensurable in length. We must show that the rectangle contained by A and B is medial.

**Step 2.** Set out a rational straight line C. Apply the square on A to C, producing breadth D, so that sq(A) = rect(C, D). Since A is medial, by 10.22 the breadth D is rational and incommensurable in length with C.

**Step 3.** By 6.1, rect(A, B) : sq(A) = B : A, since both are rectangles with one side A and the other sides B and A respectively.

**Step 4.** Since A and B are commensurable in length, the ratio B : A is a ratio of a number to a number (by 10.5). Therefore rect(A, B) and sq(A) are commensurable (by 10.6).

**Step 5.** Now apply rect(A, B) to the rational straight line C, producing breadth E, so that rect(A, B) = rect(C, E).

**Step 6.** Since rect(A, B) = rect(C, E) and sq(A) = rect(C, D), and both are applied to the same line C, by 6.1 we have rect(A, B) : sq(A) = E : D.

**Step 7.** Since rect(A, B) is commensurable with sq(A) (Step 4), and rect(A, B) : sq(A) = E : D (Step 6), by 10.11 E is commensurable in length with D.

**Step 8.** Since D is rational (Step 2) and E is commensurable in length with D (Step 7), E is rational (by D10.1.3, being commensurable with a rational straight line).

**Step 9.** Since D is incommensurable in length with C (Step 2), and E is commensurable in length with D (Step 7), by 10.13 E is incommensurable in length with C.

**Step 10.** Now C is rational and E is rational, and they are incommensurable in length (Step 9). Since both are rational, they are commensurable in square (by D10.1.3), hence they are commensurable in square only.

**Step 11.** Therefore the rectangle rect(C, E) is contained by rational straight lines commensurable in square only. By 10.21, this rectangle is irrational, and the side of the square equal to it is medial.

**Step 12.** But rect(C, E) = rect(A, B) (Step 5). Therefore the rectangle contained by A and B is medial, which is what was to be proved.

statement: The rectangle contained by medial straight lines commensurable in square only is either rational or medial.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let A and B be medial straight lines commensurable in square only. We must show that the rectangle contained by A and B is either rational or medial.

**Step 2.** Let C be a rational straight line set out. Since A is medial, the square on A is medial [by D10.1.4 and 10.21]. Apply the square on A to C, producing breadth D, so that the rectangle C times D equals the square on A. By 10.22, since the square on a medial straight line applied to a rational straight line produces as breadth a straight line rational and incommensurable in length with the line to which it is applied, D is rational and incommensurable in length with C.

**Step 3.** Now apply the rectangle A times B to the rational straight line C, producing breadth E, so that the rectangle C times E equals the rectangle A times B.

**Step 4.** Since the rectangle C times D equals A times A, and the rectangle C times E equals A times B, we have C times D is to C times E as A times A is to A times B. But rectangles sharing side A satisfy A times A : A times B = A : B [by 6.1]. Also, since both C times D and C times E lie on the same base C, we have C times D : C times E = D : E [by 6.1]. Therefore D : E = A : B.

**Step 5.** Since D : E = A : B, the duplicate ratio of D to E equals the duplicate ratio of A to B. By 6.20, the squares on proportional straight lines are in the duplicate ratio of the lines, so the square on D is to the square on E as the square on A is to the square on B.

**Step 6.** Since A and B are commensurable in square, the square on A is commensurable with the square on B [by D10.1.2]. Therefore, since the square on D is to the square on E as the square on A is to the square on B, and the square on A is commensurable with the square on B, the square on D is commensurable with the square on E [by 10.11]. Hence D and E are commensurable in square [by D10.1.2].

**Step 7.** Since D : E = A : B, and A and B are incommensurable in length (being commensurable in square only), D and E are also incommensurable in length [by 10.11].

**Step 8.** From Step 2, D is rational. From Step 6, E is commensurable in square with D. Since D is rational and E is commensurable in square with D, E is also rational [by D10.1.3]. Thus D and E are both rational and, by Step 7, incommensurable in length. Therefore D and E are either commensurable in length or commensurable in square only with the rational straight line C.

**Step 9.** Now C is rational and E is rational. There are two cases. Case 1: If C and E are commensurable in length, then the rectangle C times E is rational [by 10.19]. Since C times E equals the rectangle A times B, the rectangle A times B is rational.

**Step 10.** Case 2: If C and E are incommensurable in length, then since C and E are both rational, they are commensurable in square only. Therefore the rectangle C times E is irrational, and the side of the square equal to it is medial [by 10.21]. Hence the rectangle A times B, being equal to C times E, is medial.

**Step 11.** Since C and E are both rational, they are commensurable at least in square [by D10.1.3], so one of these two cases must hold: either they are commensurable in length or they are commensurable in square only. Therefore the rectangle contained by the medial straight lines A and B, commensurable in square only, is either rational or medial. Q.E.D.

statement: A medial area does not exceed a medial area by a rational area.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB and CD be medial areas with AB greater than CD. Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that AB exceeds CD by a rational area, so that AB minus CD is rational.

**Step 2.** Let e be a rational straight line. Apply AB to e, producing breadth p, so that the rectangle contained by e and p equals AB. Apply CD to e, producing breadth q, so that the rectangle contained by e and q equals CD.

**Step 3.** Since AB is a medial area, it is equal to the square on some medial straight line [10.21]. By 10.22, since the square on a medial straight line applied to a rational straight line produces as breadth a straight line rational and incommensurable in length with that to which it is applied, p is rational and incommensurable in length with e.

**Step 4.** Since CD is likewise a medial area, by the same reasoning [10.21, 10.22], q is rational and incommensurable in length with e.

**Step 5.** Now the rectangle contained by e and p minus the rectangle contained by e and q equals the rectangle contained by e and the line p minus q [CN3, since both rectangles share the same base e]. Thus AB minus CD equals the rectangle contained by e and the line p minus q. Since AB minus CD is rational by hypothesis, and e is rational, by 10.20 the breadth p minus q is rational and commensurable in length with e.

**Step 6.** Since p is rational, p is commensurable in square with e [D10.1.3], meaning the square on p is commensurable with the square on e [D10.1.2]. Similarly, the square on q is commensurable with the square on e. By 10.12, the square on p and the square on q are commensurable with each other.

**Step 7.** Since the square on p is commensurable with the square on q, we may write the square on p equals the square on q together with the difference of the squares on p and q. By 10.15, since the square on p is commensurable with the square on q, the difference of the squares (that is, the square on p minus the square on q) is commensurable with the square on q, and hence by 10.12, commensurable with the square on e. Thus the area equal to the square on p minus the square on q is a rational area [D10.1.4].

**Step 8.** By 2.1, the rectangle contained by the sum p plus q and the difference p minus q equals the square on p minus the square on q. For: cutting the line p plus q into segments p and q, the rectangle contained by p plus q and p minus q equals the rectangle contained by p and p minus q together with the rectangle contained by q and p minus q [2.1]. Again by 2.1, the rectangle contained by p and p minus q equals the square on p minus the rectangle contained by p and q, and the rectangle contained by q and p minus q equals the rectangle contained by p and q minus the square on q [CN2, CN3]. Adding these, the rectangle contained by p plus q and p minus q equals the square on p minus the square on q.

**Step 9.** Since the rectangle contained by p plus q and p minus q is rational [Steps 7 and 8], and since p minus q is a rational straight line [Step 5], by 10.20, the breadth p plus q is rational and commensurable in length with p minus q.

**Step 10.** Since p minus q is commensurable in length with e [Step 5], and p plus q is commensurable in length with p minus q [Step 9], by 10.12, p plus q is commensurable in length with e.

**Step 11.** Now the lines p plus q and p minus q are both commensurable in length with e [Steps 5 and 10], hence commensurable in length with each other [10.12]. Their sum equals twice p, that is, p plus q together with p minus q equals p plus p. By 10.15, since p plus q and p minus q are commensurable, their sum (which is twice p) is commensurable in length with each of them, and hence commensurable in length with e.

**Step 12.** But twice p is commensurable in length with p, since p together with p equals twice p and p is commensurable with itself, so by 10.15, twice p is commensurable with p. Since twice p is commensurable in length with e [Step 11], and twice p is commensurable in length with p, by 10.12, p is commensurable in length with e.

**Step 13.** This contradicts Step 3, which established that p is incommensurable in length with e.

**Step 14.** Therefore the assumption is false, and a medial area does not exceed a medial area by a rational area. Q.E.D.

statement: To find medial straight lines commensurable in square only which contain a rational rectangle.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let A be a rational straight line. By 10.10, find a straight line B such that B is incommensurable in length with A but commensurable in square with A. Since A is rational and B is commensurable in square with A, B is also rational by D10.1.3. Since A and B are commensurable in square but incommensurable in length, A and B are rational straight lines commensurable in square only.

**Step 2.** By 6.13, find D the mean proportional between A and B, so that A:D = D:B. Then by 6.17, the square on D equals the rectangle contained by A and B, that is, sq(D) = rect(A, B).

**Step 3.** Since A and B are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, by 10.21 the rectangle rect(A, B) is irrational, namely medial. Therefore sq(D) is a medial area, and D is a medial straight line by 10.21 and D10.1.4.

**Step 4.** By 6.12, find E as the fourth proportional to A, B, D, so that A:B = D:E.

**Step 5.** We show that D, B, E are in continuous proportion. By 5.16 (alternation), from A:B = D:E we obtain A:D = B:E. But from Step 2, A:D = D:B. Therefore D:B = B:E by CN1. Thus D, B, E are three magnitudes in continuous proportion.

**Step 6.** Since D:B = B:E, by 6.17 the rectangle contained by D and E equals the square on B, that is, rect(D, E) = sq(B). Since B is rational, sq(B) is a rational area by D10.1.4. Therefore rect(D, E) is rational.

**Step 7.** We show that D and E are incommensurable in length. Since A:B = D:E (Step 4) and A is incommensurable in length with B (Step 1), by 10.11 D is incommensurable in length with E.

**Step 8.** We show that D and E are commensurable in square. Since A:B = D:E, by 6.20 (squares being similar figures), sq(A):sq(B) = sq(D):sq(E). Now sq(A) and sq(B) are both rational areas (A and B being rational, by D10.1.4), so they are commensurable with one another. By 10.5, sq(A):sq(B) is the ratio of a number to a number. Since sq(D):sq(E) equals the same ratio, by 10.6, sq(D) and sq(E) are commensurable. Therefore D and E are commensurable in square by D10.1.2.

**Step 9.** Since D and E are incommensurable in length (Step 7) but commensurable in square (Step 8), D and E are commensurable in square only.

**Step 10.** We show that E is medial. Since D is medial (Step 3) and E is commensurable in square with D (Step 8), meaning sq(D) and sq(E) are commensurable, E is medial by 10.23.

**Step 11.** Therefore D and E are medial straight lines, commensurable in square only, which contain a rational rectangle (rect(D, E) is rational by Step 6). This is what was required to find.

statement: To find medial straight lines commensurable in square only which contain a medial rectangle.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let A be a rational straight line. Set out three numbers d, e, f with the following properties: (a) d:e is not the ratio of a square number to a square number; (b) e:f is not the ratio of a square number to a square number; (c) d:f is the ratio of a square number to a square number, say d:f = p-squared : q-squared; (d) p:q is not the ratio of a square number to a square number; (e) ep:dq is not the ratio of a square number to a square number. Such numbers exist: take d = 2, e = 3, f = 8, giving p = 1, q = 2; then 2:3 is not a square ratio, 3:8 is not a square ratio, 2:8 = 1:4 = 1-squared : 2-squared is a square ratio, 1:2 is not a square ratio, and 3:4 is not a square ratio.

**Step 2.** Let it be contrived that d:e = sq(A):sq(B) [6.12]. Since d:e is a ratio of numbers, sq(A) and sq(B) are commensurable [10.6], so A and B are commensurable in square. Since d:e is not a ratio of square numbers, A and B are incommensurable in length [10.9]. Since B is commensurable in square with the rational straight line A, B is rational [D10.1.3]. Therefore A and B are rational straight lines commensurable in square only.

**Step 3.** Let it be contrived that e:f = sq(B):sq(C) [6.12]. By the same reasoning as Step 2, since e:f is a ratio of numbers but not of square numbers, B and C are rational straight lines commensurable in square only [10.6, 10.9, D10.1.3].

**Step 4.** Since d:e = sq(A):sq(B) and e:f = sq(B):sq(C), by ex aequali, d:f = sq(A):sq(C) [5.22]. Since d:f = p-squared : q-squared is the ratio of a square number to a square number, A and C are commensurable in length [10.9].

**Step 5.** By 6.20, sq(A):sq(C) is the duplicate ratio of A:C. By 8.11, p-squared : q-squared is the duplicate ratio of p:q. Since sq(A):sq(C) = p-squared : q-squared [Step 4], the duplicate of A:C equals the duplicate of p:q, and therefore A:C = p:q.

**Step 6.** Let G be the mean proportional between A and B [6.13], so that sq(G) = rect(A, B) [6.17]. Since A and B are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, rect(A, B) is irrational and G is a medial straight line [10.21].

**Step 7.** Let H be the mean proportional between B and C [6.13], so that sq(H) = rect(B, C) [6.17]. Since B and C are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, rect(B, C) is irrational and H is a medial straight line [10.21].

**Step 8.** Since sq(G) = rect(A, B) and sq(H) = rect(B, C), these rectangles share the common side B. By 6.1, sq(G):sq(H) = A:C = p:q [Step 5]. Since p:q is a ratio of numbers, sq(G) is commensurable with sq(H) [10.6], so G and H are commensurable in square. Since p:q is not a ratio of square numbers [condition (d)], G and H are incommensurable in length [10.9]. Therefore G and H are commensurable in square only.

**Step 9.** Let K be the mean proportional between A and C [6.13], so that sq(K) = rect(A, C) [6.17]. Since A and C are rational and commensurable in length [Step 4], rect(A, C) is rational [10.19]. Now sq(K):sq(A) = rect(A, C):rect(A, A) = C:A [6.1], and since A and C are commensurable in length, C:A is a ratio of numbers [10.5], so sq(K) is commensurable with sq(A) [10.6]. Therefore K is rational [D10.1.3].

**Step 10.** Now sq(A):sq(G) = rect(A, A):rect(A, B) = A:B [6.1], and sq(K):sq(H) = rect(A, C):rect(B, C) = A:B [6.1]. Therefore sq(A):sq(G) = sq(K):sq(H) [CN1]. By alternation, sq(A):sq(K) = sq(G):sq(H) [5.16]. Since squares are similar figures described on the respective lines, by the converse of 6.22, A:K = G:H.

**Step 11.** By alternation, A:G = K:H [5.16]. From the mean proportional construction, sq(G) = rect(A, B) implies A:G = G:B [6.17]. Therefore G:B = K:H [CN1]. By 6.16, since four straight lines G, B, K, H are proportional (G:B = K:H), the rectangle contained by the extremes equals the rectangle contained by the means: rect(G, H) = rect(B, K).

**Step 12.** Since G and H are medial straight lines commensurable in square only [Steps 6, 7, 8], by 10.25, rect(G, H) is either rational or medial. Suppose for contradiction that rect(G, H) is rational. Then rect(B, K) is rational [Step 11]. The area rect(B, K) is the rectangle contained by B and K; applying this rational area to the rational straight line B, the breadth is K. By 10.20, K would be commensurable in length with B.

**Step 13.** However, from Step 2 (inverted), sq(B):sq(A) = e:d. By 7.17, multiplying both terms by p gives ep:dp = e:d, so sq(B):sq(A) = ep:dp. From Step 9, sq(A):sq(K) = A:C = p:q [6.1, Step 5]. By 7.17, multiplying both terms by d gives dp:dq = p:q, so sq(A):sq(K) = dp:dq. Since the middle terms now agree, by ex aequali, sq(B):sq(K) = ep:dq [5.22]. Since ep:dq is not the ratio of a square number to a square number [condition (e)], B and K are incommensurable in length [10.9]. This contradicts the conclusion of Step 12 that K is commensurable in length with B.

**Step 14.** Therefore rect(G, H) is not rational, and hence by 10.25 it is medial. Thus G and H are medial straight lines commensurable in square only which contain a medial rectangle, which is what was required to find. Q.E.D.

statement: To find two rational straight lines commensurable in square only and such that the square on the greater is greater than the square on the less by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with the greater.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let A be a rational straight line set out. Let there be found two square numbers, say 9 and 4, such that their difference, 9 - 4 = 5, is not a square number. (For 9 = 3 times 3 and 4 = 2 times 2 are square numbers, and 5 is not a square number.)

**Step 2.** Then the ratio 9 : 5 is a ratio of a number to a number but is not a ratio of a square number to a square number, since 9 is square but 5 is not square.

**Step 3.** Now let it be contrived that 9 : 5 = sq(A) : sq(B), where B is some straight line. Since sq(A) is rational (for A is rational and the square on a rational line is rational by D10.1.4), and sq(A) : sq(B) = 9 : 5, a ratio of number to number, therefore sq(A) and sq(B) are commensurable by 10.6. Therefore sq(B) is also rational. Therefore B is rational by D10.1.3.

**Step 4.** Since sq(A) : sq(B) = 9 : 5, and 9 : 5 is not a ratio of a square number to a square number, therefore A and B are incommensurable in length by 10.9.

**Step 5.** But sq(A) and sq(B) are commensurable (as shown in Step 3), so A and B are commensurable in square by D10.1.2. Therefore A and B are rational straight lines commensurable in square only.

**Step 6.** Now since sq(A) : sq(B) = 9 : 5, by separation of the ratio (5.17), sq(A) - sq(B) : sq(B) = 4 : 5. Therefore by inversion, sq(B) : sq(A) - sq(B) = 5 : 4.

**Step 7.** And since sq(A) : sq(B) = 9 : 5, we also have, componendo via the ratio, sq(A) : sq(A) - sq(B) = 9 : 4. For since sq(A) : sq(B) = 9 : 5, and sq(A) - sq(B) corresponds to the excess, we compute: sq(A) - sq(B) : sq(A) = (9 - 5) : 9 = 4 : 9 by 5.19 (separation applied to the inverse). Hence sq(A) : sq(A) - sq(B) = 9 : 4.

**Step 8.** Now 9 and 4 are both square numbers (9 = 3 times 3 and 4 = 2 times 2). Therefore sq(A) : sq(A) - sq(B) is a ratio of a square number to a square number.

**Step 9.** Since A is greater than B (for sq(A) > sq(B) as 9 > 5), the square on A is greater than the square on B by some square, say the square on C, so that sq(A) = sq(B) + sq(C), that is, sq(C) = sq(A) - sq(B).

**Step 10.** Therefore sq(A) : sq(C) = 9 : 4, which is a ratio of a square number to a square number. Therefore by 10.9, A is commensurable in length with C.

**Step 11.** Therefore the square on A is greater than the square on B by the square on a straight line C commensurable in length with A.

**Step 12.** Thus A and B have been found as two rational straight lines commensurable in square only such that the square on the greater, A, is greater than the square on the less, B, by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with A. Q.E.F.

statement: To find two rational straight lines commensurable in square only and such that the square on the greater is greater is greater than the square on the less by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with the greater.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let the rational straight line A be set out, and let there be found two square numbers CD and DE such that their sum CE is not a square number. Such numbers exist: for example, let CD = 4 and DE = 9, so that CE = 13, which is not a square number.

**Step 2.** Let it be contrived that CE is to CD as the square on A is to the square on a straight line B. This is possible since, given the ratio of two numbers, we can find a straight line whose square has a given ratio to the square on a given line.

**Step 3.** Since CE and CD are both numbers, the ratio CE to CD is the ratio of a number to a number. Therefore the square on A has to the square on B the ratio which a number has to a number. By 10.6, the squares on A and B are commensurable, hence A and B are commensurable in square.

**Step 4.** Now CE is not a square number, while CD is a square number. Therefore the ratio CE to CD is not the ratio of a square number to a square number. Hence the square on A does not have to the square on B the ratio of a square number to a square number. By 10.9, A and B are incommensurable in length.

**Step 5.** Since A is rational and B is commensurable in square with A, B is also rational by D10.1.3. Combined with Step 4, A and B are rational straight lines commensurable in square only.

**Step 6.** Since the square on A is to the square on B as CE is to CD, by separation (5.17), the square on A minus the square on B is to the square on B as DE is to CD. That is, if F is the straight line such that the square on F equals the difference of the squares on A and B, then the square on F is to the square on B as DE is to CD.

**Step 7.** Equivalently, since CE is to CD as the square on A is to the square on B, we also have CE is to DE as the square on A is to the square on F (by 5.17 applied in the form: the whole to the remainder equals the whole to the remainder). Now DE is a square number and CE is not a square number. Therefore the ratio CE to DE is not the ratio of a square number to a square number. Hence the square on A does not have to the square on F the ratio of a square number to a square number. By 10.9, A and F are incommensurable in length.

**Step 8.** But the square on A is greater than the square on B by the square on F (by construction in Step 6). Therefore the square on the greater line A exceeds the square on the lesser line B by the square on a straight line F which is incommensurable in length with A.

**Step 9.** Therefore two rational straight lines A and B have been found, commensurable in square only, such that the square on the greater is greater than the square on the less by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with the greater. Q.E.F.

statement: To find two medial straight lines commensurable in square only, containing a rational rectangle, and such that the square on the greater is greater than the square on the less by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with the greater.
proof:
**Step 1.** By Proposition 10.29, find two rational straight lines A and B, commensurable in square only, with A greater than B, such that the square on A is greater than the square on B by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with A.

**Step 2.** By Proposition 6.13, take C as a mean proportional between A and B, so that A is to C as C is to B, and the square on C equals the rectangle contained by A and B.

**Step 3.** Since A and B are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, by Proposition 10.21 the rectangle contained by A and B is irrational, and the side of the square equal to it is medial. Since the square on C equals this rectangle, C is medial.

**Step 4.** By Proposition 6.12, take D as the fourth proportional to A, B, C, so that A is to B as C is to D.

**Step 5.** We show that D is medial. From A is to B as C is to D, by Proposition 6.22, the square on A is to the square on B as the square on C is to the square on D. Now since A and B are rational, the squares on A and on B are both rational areas, hence both are commensurable with the square on the assigned rational straight line, and therefore commensurable with each other by Proposition 10.12. Since the square on A is commensurable with the square on B, and the square on A is to the square on B as the square on C is to the square on D, by Proposition 10.11 the square on C is commensurable with the square on D.
