**Step 29.** Apply all four quantities to the rational line FG. Let sq(CB) + sq(BD) applied to FG give breadth LM; let 2*rect(CB,BD) applied to FG give breadth MN. Let sq(CE) + sq(BE) applied to FG give breadth LP; let 2*rect(CE,BE) applied to FG give breadth PQ.

**Step 30.** Since sq(CB) + sq(BD) = 2*rect(CB,BD) + sq(AB) (from 2.7 applied to CB = AB + BD), the rectangle FG by LM = FG by MN + sq(AB). Hence FG by (LM - MN) = sq(AB), so the breadth (LM - MN) applied to FG equals the square on AB.

**Step 31.** Similarly, FG by (LP - PQ) = sq(AB). Therefore FG by (LM - MN) = FG by (LP - PQ), and so LM - MN = LP - PQ (6.1, CN1).

**Step 32.** Now LM is rational and incommensurable in length with FG (Step 9, 10.22). MN is rational and incommensurable in length with FG (Step 11, 10.22). And LM is incommensurable with MN, since sq(CB) + sq(BD) is incommensurable with 2*rect(CB,BD) (Step 28), so by 10.11 the breadths are incommensurable.

**Step 33.** Therefore LM and MN are rational straight lines commensurable in square only (they are both rational, and incommensurable in length by Step 32). Hence LM - MN is an apotome (10.73).

**Step 34.** By the same reasoning, LP and PQ are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, so LP - PQ is an apotome (10.73).

**Step 35.** From Step 31, LM - MN = LP - PQ. Both are apotomes. And FG by (LM - MN) = sq(AB), meaning the square on AB equals a rational line (FG) times an apotome.

**Step 36.** Now suppose the sums of squares are not equal, i.e., LM is not equal to LP. Then from LM - MN = LP - PQ, we get LM - LP = MN - PQ. The left side is the difference of two rational lines (breadths of medial areas applied to FG). But LM is the breadth of the sum sq(CB) + sq(BD), and LP is the breadth of sq(CE) + sq(BE), both medial areas. If LM does not equal LP, then MN does not equal PQ.

**Step 37.** From Step 31, the apotome LM - MN equals the apotome LP - PQ. By 10.79, an apotome has a unique annex: there is only one rational line commensurable in square only with the whole that can be subtracted. So if LM - MN and LP - PQ represent the same apotome, then the decomposition is unique.

**Step 38.** The apotome LM - MN has whole LM and annex MN. The apotome LP - PQ has whole LP and annex PQ. Since these two expressions equal the same apotome, by 10.79, LM = LP and MN = PQ.

**Step 39.** From LM = LP: FG by LM = FG by LP, so sq(CB) + sq(BD) = sq(CE) + sq(BE) (CN1).

**Step 40.** From MN = PQ: FG by MN = FG by PQ, so 2*rect(CB,BD) = 2*rect(CE,BE), and therefore rect(CB,BD) = rect(CE,BE) (CN3).

**Step 41.** From Step 5: CB + BE = CE + BD. Squaring by 2.4: sq(CB) + 2*rect(CB,BE) + sq(BE) = sq(CE) + 2*rect(CE,BD) + sq(BD).

**Step 42.** Rearranging: (sq(CB) + sq(BE)) - (sq(CE) + sq(BD)) = 2*rect(CE,BD) - 2*rect(CB,BE).

**Step 43.** From Step 39: sq(CB) + sq(BD) = sq(CE) + sq(BE), which gives sq(CB) - sq(CE) = sq(BE) - sq(BD). Therefore sq(CB) + sq(BE) - sq(CE) - sq(BD) = 2*(sq(BE) - sq(BD)). So the left side of Step 42 equals 2*(sq(BE) - sq(BD)).

**Step 44.** For the right side: rect(CE,BD) and rect(CB,BE). From Step 40, rect(CB,BD) = rect(CE,BE), so CB/CE = BE/BD (6.16). Let this common ratio be r. Then CB = r*CE and BE = r*BD (in the sense of proportion).

**Step 45.** Substituting into CB + BE = CE + BD (Step 5): r*CE + r*BD = CE + BD, so r*(CE + BD) = CE + BD. Since CE + BD is nonzero (both are positive magnitudes), we get r = 1, meaning CB = CE and BD = BE.

**Step 46.** But if BD = BE, the two annexes are the same, contradicting our assumption that they are different. Therefore the supposition that two different annexes exist is false.

**Step 47.** Hence, to a second apotome of a medial straight line, only one medial straight line can be annexed which is commensurable with the whole in square only and which contains with the whole a medial rectangle. Q.E.D.

statement: To a minor straight line only one straight line can be annexed which is incommensurable in square with the whole and which makes, with the whole, the sum of the squares on them rational but twice the rectangle contained by them medial.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be a minor straight line, and let BC be the annex to it, so that AC is the whole. Then by the definition of a minor straight line [10.76], AC and BC are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AC and BC is rational, and the rectangle contained by AC and BC is medial (so that twice the rectangle AC, BC is also medial).

**Step 2.** Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that BD is another straight line annexed to AB, different from BC, such that AD and BD are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AD and BD is rational, and twice the rectangle contained by AD and BD is medial.

**Step 3.** Since AC is the whole and BC the annex, the line AC is cut at B into segments AB and BC. By 2.7, the square on AC together with the square on BC equals twice the rectangle contained by AC and BC together with the square on AB. That is, sq(AC) + sq(BC) = 2*rect(AC, BC) + sq(AB).

**Step 4.** Similarly, since AD is the whole and BD the annex, the line AD is cut at B into segments AB and BD. By 2.7, sq(AD) + sq(BD) = 2*rect(AD, BD) + sq(AB).

**Step 5.** Since both expressions equal sq(AB) plus their respective double rectangles, by CN1 we obtain: sq(AC) + sq(BC) - 2*rect(AC, BC) = sq(AD) + sq(BD) - 2*rect(AD, BD). Rearranging by CN3: [sq(AC) + sq(BC)] - [sq(AD) + sq(BD)] = 2*rect(AC, BC) - 2*rect(AD, BD).

**Step 6.** Now, sq(AC) + sq(BC) is rational and sq(AD) + sq(BD) is rational. Since both are rational areas, each is commensurable with the square on the assigned rational straight line [D10.1.4]. Therefore by 10.12 they are commensurable with one another.

**Step 7.** Suppose the two sums of squares are unequal. Without loss of generality, assume sq(AC) + sq(BC) > sq(AD) + sq(BD). Then from Step 5, 2*rect(AC, BC) > 2*rect(AD, BD), and the excess 2*rect(AC, BC) - 2*rect(AD, BD) equals the rational difference [sq(AC) + sq(BC)] - [sq(AD) + sq(BD)]. Since the two rational areas are commensurable with each other (Step 6), their difference, being the remainder when commensurable magnitudes are subtracted, is commensurable with them [10.15], and hence is itself a rational area [D10.1.4].

**Step 8.** But 2*rect(AC, BC) is medial and 2*rect(AD, BD) is medial. Thus a medial area would exceed a medial area by a rational area. This contradicts 10.26, which states that a medial area does not exceed a medial area by a rational area.

**Step 9.** Therefore the assumption in Step 7 is false, and sq(AC) + sq(BC) = sq(AD) + sq(BD). It follows immediately from Step 5 that 2*rect(AC, BC) = 2*rect(AD, BD), and hence rect(AC, BC) = rect(AD, BD).

**Step 10.** Since sq(AC) + sq(BC) = sq(AD) + sq(BD) and rect(AC, BC) = rect(AD, BD), we apply 2.4: the square on the sum AC + BC equals sq(AC) + sq(BC) + 2*rect(AC, BC) = sq(AD) + sq(BD) + 2*rect(AD, BD) = the square on the sum AD + BD. Therefore AC + BC = AD + BD.

**Step 11.** We also know from the construction that AC - BC = AB = AD - BD.

**Step 12.** Adding the equalities from Steps 10 and 11 by CN2: (AC + BC) + (AC - BC) = (AD + BD) + (AD - BD), that is, twice AC = twice AD, so AC = AD.

**Step 13.** Subtracting: from AC - BC = AD - BD and AC = AD, by CN3 we conclude BC = BD.

**Step 14.** Therefore the annex BC is the same as BD, and to a minor straight line only one straight line can be annexed which is incommensurable in square with the whole and which makes, with the whole, the sum of the squares on them rational but twice the rectangle contained by them medial. Q.E.D.

statement: To a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole only one straight line can be annexed which is incommensurable in square with the whole straight line and which with the whole straight line makes the sum of the squares on them medial, but twice the rectangle contained by them rational.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole, and let CB be annexed to it, so that AC is the whole and AB = AC - CB. Then by the definition of this irrational line (10.77), AC and CB are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AC and CB is medial, and twice the rectangle contained by AC and CB is rational.

**Step 2.** Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that another straight line BD, different from CB, can also be annexed to AB so that AD is the whole and AB = AD - DB, with AD and DB satisfying the same conditions: AD and DB are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AD and DB is medial, and twice the rectangle contained by AD and DB is rational.

**Step 3.** Since twice the rectangle AC.CB is rational, and twice the rectangle AD.DB is also rational, these two areas are commensurable with one another, for rational areas are commensurable with one another (D10.1.4, 10.12).

**Step 4.** Now, by 2.7, the square on AC equals the sum of the square on AB, the square on CB, and twice the rectangle AB.CB. Therefore twice the rectangle AC.CB equals the square on AC minus the square on CB minus the square on AB, rearranging. More precisely, the squares on AC and CB together equal the square on AB plus twice the rectangle AC.CB (by 2.7 applied to AC = AB + CB: sq(AC) = sq(AB) + sq(CB) + 2*rect(AB,CB), so sq(AC) + sq(CB) = sq(AB) + 2*sq(CB) + 2*rect(AB,CB)). Let us proceed more directly.

**Step 5.** By 2.7, since AC = AB + BC, we have the square on AC equal to the squares on AB and BC together with twice the rectangle AB.BC. Similarly, since AD = AB + BD, the square on AD equals the squares on AB and BD together with twice the rectangle AB.BD.

**Step 6.** Therefore the squares on AC and CB taken together equal the square on AB plus two times the square on CB plus twice the rectangle AB.CB, which by rearrangement gives: sq(AC) + sq(CB) = sq(AB) + 2*sq(CB) + 2*rect(AB,CB). Likewise, sq(AD) + sq(DB) = sq(AB) + 2*sq(DB) + 2*rect(AB,DB).

**Step 7.** Now twice the rectangle AC.CB is rational and twice the rectangle AD.DB is rational, so by subtraction: [sq(AC) + sq(CB)] - 2*rect(AC,CB) = sq(AB) = [sq(AD) + sq(DB)] - 2*rect(AD,DB). This means sq(AC) + sq(CB) - 2*rect(AC,CB) = sq(AD) + sq(DB) - 2*rect(AD,DB).

**Step 8.** Therefore [sq(AC) + sq(CB)] - [sq(AD) + sq(DB)] = 2*rect(AC,CB) - 2*rect(AD,DB) (CN2, CN3).

**Step 9.** The left side, [sq(AC) + sq(CB)] - [sq(AD) + sq(DB)], is the difference of two medial areas (since both sums of squares are medial by hypothesis). The right side, 2*rect(AC,CB) - 2*rect(AD,DB), is the difference of two rational areas (since both double rectangles are rational by hypothesis).

**Step 10.** If the left side is not zero, then a medial area exceeds (or falls short of) a medial area by a rational area, which contradicts 10.26, which states that a medial area does not exceed a medial area by a rational area.

**Step 11.** Therefore the left side must be zero: sq(AC) + sq(CB) = sq(AD) + sq(DB). And consequently the right side must also be zero: 2*rect(AC,CB) = 2*rect(AD,DB).

**Step 12.** Since sq(AC) + sq(CB) = sq(AD) + sq(DB), and also 2*rect(AC,CB) = 2*rect(AD,DB), we add these equalities: [sq(AC) + sq(CB)] + 2*rect(AC,CB) = [sq(AD) + sq(DB)] + 2*rect(AD,DB). By 2.4, the left side equals the square on (AC + CB) and the right side equals the square on (AD + DB). Therefore the square on (AC + CB) equals the square on (AD + DB), whence AC + CB = AD + DB (CN1).

**Step 13.** Similarly, by subtraction: [sq(AC) + sq(CB)] - 2*rect(AC,CB) = [sq(AD) + sq(DB)] - 2*rect(AD,DB). By 2.7, the left side equals the square on (AC - CB) and the right side equals the square on (AD - DB). But AC - CB = AB = AD - DB. So this is consistent and holds automatically.

**Step 14.** From Step 12, AC + CB = AD + DB. From the hypothesis, AC - CB = AB = AD - DB. Adding these two equations: 2*AC = 2*AD, so AC = AD (CN2, CN1). Subtracting: 2*CB = 2*DB, so CB = DB.

**Step 15.** Therefore the same straight line CB is annexed, and no other line BD different from CB can satisfy the conditions. This proves that to a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole, only one straight line can be annexed which is incommensurable in square with the whole and which with the whole makes the sum of squares medial but twice the rectangle rational. Q.E.D.

statement: To a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole only one straight line can be annexed which is incommensurable in square with the whole straight line and which with the whole straight line makes the sum of the squares on them medial and twice the rectangle contained by them both medial and also incommensurable with the sum of the squares on them.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole, and let BC be annexed to it, so that AC is incommensurable in square with BC, the sum of the squares on AC and CB is medial, twice the rectangle AC by CB is medial, and the sum of the squares on AC and CB is incommensurable with twice the rectangle AC by CB [10.78]. I say that no other straight line besides BC can be annexed to AB fulfilling these conditions.

**Step 2.** For, if possible, let BD also be annexed to AB, so that AD is also incommensurable in square with DB, the sum of the squares on AD and DB is medial, twice the rectangle AD by DB is medial, and the sum of the squares on AD and DB is incommensurable with twice the rectangle AD by DB [10.78].

**Step 3.** Set out a rational straight line EF. Apply to EF the rectangle EG equal to the sum of the squares on AC and CB, producing EM as breadth [1.45]. Subtract from EG the rectangle HG equal to twice the rectangle AC by CB, producing HM as breadth. Then the remainder EH equals the square on AB [2.7], so that EH is the rectangle applied to EF producing EH with breadth equal to the square on AB divided by EF.

**Step 4.** Since the sum of the squares on AC and CB is medial and equals EG, the rectangle EG is medial. And it is applied to the rational straight line EF, so EM is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [10.22].

**Step 5.** Since twice the rectangle AC by CB is medial and equals HG, the rectangle HG is also medial. And it is applied to the rational straight line EF, so HM is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [10.22].

**Step 6.** Since the sum of the squares on AC and CB is incommensurable with twice the rectangle AC by CB, the rectangle EG is incommensurable with the rectangle HG. Therefore EM is incommensurable in length with HM [6.1, 10.11].

**Step 7.** Both EM and HM are rational. Therefore EM and HM are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. Therefore EH is an apotome [10.73], with HM as its annex.

**Step 8.** Similarly, apply to EF the rectangle EI equal to the sum of the squares on AD and DB, producing EN as breadth. Since the square on AB also equals the remainder when twice the rectangle AD by DB is subtracted from the sum of the squares on AD and DB [2.7], the rectangle EH also equals the square on AB from this decomposition. But EH was also obtained from the first decomposition. Thus EI minus the rectangle equal to twice the rectangle AD by DB equals EG minus HG, that is, they both equal EH.

**Step 9.** Apply to EF the rectangle equal to twice the rectangle AD by DB, and let this equal the rectangle with breadth HN (that is, subtract from EI the rectangle equal to twice the rectangle AD by DB to obtain EH). Then EN is the breadth produced by the sum of the squares on AD and DB applied to EF.

**Step 10.** Since the sum of the squares on AD and DB is medial and equals EI, the rectangle EI is medial. And it is applied to the rational straight line EF, so EN is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [10.22].

**Step 11.** Since twice the rectangle AD by DB is medial and is applied to the rational straight line EF producing HN as breadth, HN is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [10.22].

**Step 12.** Since the sum of the squares on AD and DB is incommensurable with twice the rectangle AD by DB, the area EI is incommensurable with the area producing breadth HN. Therefore EN is incommensurable in length with HN [6.1, 10.11].

**Step 13.** Both EN and HN are rational. Therefore EN and HN are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. Therefore EH is an apotome with HN as its annex [10.73].

**Step 14.** But EH was already shown to be an apotome with HM as its annex [Step 7]. By 10.79, to an apotome only one rational straight line can be annexed which is commensurable with the whole in square only. Therefore HM equals HN.

**Step 15.** Now, since EG equals the sum of the squares on AC and CB, and EI equals the sum of the squares on AD and DB, and EH equals the square on AB in both cases, the remainder HG equals twice the rectangle AC by CB and the corresponding remainder from EI equals twice the rectangle AD by DB.

**Step 16.** Since the squares on AC and CB equal the squares on AD and DB plus the difference EG minus EI (or vice versa), and twice the rectangle AC by CB and twice the rectangle AD by DB are related correspondingly, we examine the areas. We have EG minus HG equals EI minus the area for twice rect(AD,DB), both equaling EH. Since HM equals HN [Step 14], the areas HG and the rectangle for twice rect(AD,DB) have the same breadth on EF from H, so HG equals twice rect(AD,DB). Therefore EG equals EI, which means the sum of squares on AC, CB equals the sum of squares on AD, DB.

**Step 17.** Since the sum of the squares on AC and CB equals the sum of the squares on AD and DB, and twice the rectangle AC by CB equals twice the rectangle AD by DB, it follows that the square on AC plus the square on CB equals the square on AD plus the square on DB, and the rectangle AC by CB equals the rectangle AD by DB.

**Step 18.** Therefore the square on AC minus the square on AD equals the square on DB minus the square on CB. Also, since AC squared plus CB squared equals AD squared plus DB squared, and these sums are both medial areas equal to one another, and similarly twice rect(AC,CB) equals twice rect(AD,DB), consider the identity: (AC + CB) squared equals the sum of squares on AC, CB plus twice rect(AC,CB), and similarly (AD + DB) squared equals the sum of squares on AD, DB plus twice rect(AD,DB) [2.4]. Since the respective parts are equal, (AC + CB) squared equals (AD + DB) squared, so AC + CB equals AD + DB.

**Step 19.** But also, since AC - CB = AB = AD - DB (both decompositions yield AB as the remainder), we have AC - CB = AD - DB.

**Step 20.** From AC + CB = AD + DB [Step 18] and AC - CB = AD - DB [Step 19], adding these equalities gives 2AC = 2AD, so AC = AD [CN2, CN3]. Subtracting then gives CB = DB, hence BC = BD.

**Step 21.** Therefore to AB, a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole, only one straight line BC can be annexed which is incommensurable in square with the whole and which with the whole makes the sum of the squares on them medial and twice the rectangle contained by them medial and also incommensurable with the sum of the squares on them. Q.E.D.

statement: To find the first apotome.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let A be a rational straight line set out. We seek to construct a first apotome.

**Step 2.** Let BG be a straight line commensurable in length with A, so that BG is also rational [D10.1.3].

**Step 3.** By Proposition 10.29, find two rational straight lines BG and GC that are commensurable in square only, such that the square on BG is greater than the square on GC by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with BG. (Proposition 10.29 provides exactly such a construction: two rational straight lines commensurable in square only where the square on the greater exceeds the square on the lesser by the square on a line commensurable with the greater.)

**Step 4.** Since BG and GC are commensurable in square only, they are incommensurable in length [D10.1.3]. Since BG and GC are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and BG is greater than GC (as the square on BG exceeds the square on GC), the remainder BC = BG - GC is an apotome, by Proposition 10.73.

**Step 5.** We now verify the conditions for BC to be a first apotome according to D10.3.1. The whole of the apotome BC is BG (the whole), and the annex is GC. We need: (i) the square on BG is greater than the square on GC by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with BG, and (ii) BG is commensurable in length with the rational straight line A set out.

**Step 6.** Condition (i): By our construction in Step 3, the square on BG is greater than the square on GC by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with BG. This is guaranteed by 10.29.

**Step 7.** Condition (ii): By Step 2, BG was chosen to be commensurable in length with A.

**Step 8.** Since both conditions of D10.3.1 are satisfied, BC is a first apotome.

**Step 9.** Therefore, the first apotome BC has been found, which is what was required.

statement: To find the second apotome.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let A be a rational straight line set out. [D10.1.3]

**Step 2.** Find three numbers DN, MN, DM such that DN = DM + MN, where DN has to DM the ratio of a square number to a square number, but neither DM to MN nor DN to MN is the ratio of a square number to a square number. For example, take DN = 9, DM = 4, MN = 5: then DN:DM = 9:4 (a ratio of square numbers), DM:MN = 4:5 (not square to square), and DN:MN = 9:5 (not square to square).

**Step 3.** Let it be contrived that sq(A):sq(GH) = DN:DM. Since DN:DM = 9:4 is the ratio of a square number to a square number, A is commensurable in length with GH. [10.9] Since A is rational, GH is also rational. [D10.1.3]

**Step 4.** Let it be contrived that sq(GH):sq(KG) = MN:DN, so that sq(KG):sq(GH) = DN:MN. Since DN:MN is a ratio of number to number, KG is commensurable in square with GH. [10.6] But DN:MN = 9:5 is not a ratio of a square number to a square number, so KG is incommensurable in length with GH. [10.9] Therefore KG and GH are commensurable in square only. Since GH is rational, KG is also rational. [D10.1.3]

**Step 5.** Since KG and GH are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, KG - GH is an apotome. [10.73] Let the apotome be called KB, where KB = KG - GH (that is, B is the point on KG such that BG = GH, and KB is the remainder).

**Step 6.** Now, sq(A):sq(KG) can be found from the chain sq(A):sq(GH) = DN:DM and sq(GH):sq(KG) = MN:DN. By the ratio ex aequali, sq(A):sq(KG) = (DN:DM) composed with (MN:DN) = MN:DM = 5:4. [5.22] Since MN:DM = 5:4 is not the ratio of a square number to a square number, A is incommensurable in length with KG. [10.9]

**Step 7.** But GH (the annex) is commensurable in length with A (from Step 3). So the annex is commensurable in length with the rational straight line set out. [D10.3.2 condition on the annex]

**Step 8.** Since sq(KG):sq(GH) = DN:MN, we have sq(KG) - sq(GH) : sq(KG) = (DN - MN) : DN = DM : DN. [5.17] That is, sq(KG) - sq(GH) has to sq(KG) the ratio DM:DN. Let sq(KG) - sq(GH) = sq(L). Then sq(L):sq(KG) = DM:DN = 4:9, which is the ratio of a square number to a square number. Therefore L is commensurable in length with KG. [10.9]

**Step 9.** Hence the square on the whole KG is greater than the square on the annex GH by the square on a straight line L commensurable in length with KG. [D10.3.2 condition on the excess]

**Step 10.** The annex GH is commensurable in length with the rational straight line A set out (Step 7), and the square on the whole KG exceeds the square on the annex GH by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with KG (Step 9). Therefore, by Definition D10.3.2, the apotome KB is a second apotome.

**Step 11.** Therefore the second apotome KB has been found. Q.E.F.

statement: To find the third apotome.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let a rational straight line A be set out, and let three positive integers E, BC, CD be taken such that: (i) BC:CD is not a ratio of a square number to a square number, (ii) E:BC is not a ratio of a square number to a square number, (iii) E:CD is not a ratio of a square number to a square number, and (iv) (BC - CD):BC is a ratio of a square number to a square number. Such numbers can be found; for example, E = 3, BC = 8, CD = 6 satisfy all four conditions.

**Step 2.** Let it be contrived that as E is to BC, so is the square on A to the square on FG. Since E:BC is not a ratio of a square number to a square number, the square on A does not have to the square on FG the ratio of a square number to a square number. Therefore A is incommensurable in length with FG. [10.9]

**Step 3.** Since E:BC is a ratio of number to number, the square on A is commensurable with the square on FG. [10.6] Since the square on A is rational, the square on FG is also rational. [D10.1.4] Therefore FG is rational. [D10.1.3] Since A is incommensurable in length with FG (Step 2), the line FG is rational and incommensurable in length with the assigned rational straight line A.

**Step 4.** Let it be contrived that as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH. Since BC:CD is not a ratio of a square number to a square number, FG is incommensurable in length with GH. [10.9] But BC:CD is a ratio of number to number, so the square on FG is commensurable with the square on GH. [10.6] Therefore FG and GH are commensurable in square only. Since the square on FG is rational, the square on GH is also rational, and therefore GH is rational. [D10.1.4, D10.1.3]

**Step 5.** Since as E is to BC, so is the square on A to the square on FG, and as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH, then ex aequali, as E is to CD, so is the square on A to the square on GH. [5.22] Since E:CD is not a ratio of a square number to a square number (condition (iii)), the square on A does not have to the square on GH the ratio of a square number to a square number. Therefore A is incommensurable in length with GH. [10.9] So GH is rational and incommensurable in length with A.

**Step 6.** Since FG and GH are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, the difference FG - GH is an apotome. [10.73]

**Step 7.** It remains to show that the square on FG exceeds the square on GH by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with FG. Since as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH, by separation of ratio, as (BC - CD) is to CD, so is (the square on FG minus the square on GH) to the square on GH. [5.17] Therefore also as BC is to (BC - CD), so is the square on FG to (the square on FG minus the square on GH). Since (BC - CD):BC is a ratio of a square number to a square number (condition (iv)), so is BC:(BC - CD). Therefore the square on FG has to the square on FG minus the square on GH the ratio of a square number to a square number. Let the square on FG minus the square on GH equal the square on K. Then the square on FG has to the square on K the ratio of a square number to a square number, so FG is commensurable in length with K. [10.9] Hence the square on FG is greater than the square on GH by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with FG.

**Step 8.** We have established: FG - GH is an apotome (Step 6); neither FG nor GH is commensurable in length with the assigned rational straight line A (Steps 3 and 5); and the square on FG exceeds the square on GH by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with FG (Step 7). By the definition of a third apotome, FG - GH is a third apotome. [D10.3.3]

**Step 9.** Therefore the third apotome has been found. Q.E.F.

statement: To find the fourth apotome.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let a rational straight line E be set out, and let BG be a straight line commensurable in length with E; then BG is also rational [D10.1.3].

**Step 2.** By Proposition 10.30, find two rational straight lines BG and DG that are commensurable in square only, such that the square on BG is greater than the square on DG by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with BG [10.30].

**Step 3.** Since BG and DG are rational and commensurable in square only, their difference BG - DG is an apotome [10.73]. Let this apotome be denoted AB, so that AB = BG - DG, where BG is the whole and DG is the annex.

**Step 4.** Since BG and DG are commensurable in square only, they are incommensurable in length [D10.1.1]. Since DG is rational (being commensurable in square with the rational line BG), DG is incommensurable in length with BG. Since BG is commensurable in length with E, and DG is incommensurable in length with BG, then DG is incommensurable in length with E [10.13].

**Step 5.** Now, BG is commensurable in length with E, which is the rational straight line set out, so the whole BG is commensurable in length with the rational straight line set out [D10.1.3].

**Step 6.** By construction in Step 2, the square on BG is greater than the square on DG by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with BG [10.30].

**Step 7.** By Definition D10.3.4, since AB is an apotome with whole BG and annex DG, and the square on the whole BG is greater than the square on the annex DG by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with the whole BG, and the whole BG is commensurable in length with the rational straight line E set out, the apotome AB is a fourth apotome [D10.3.4].

**Step 8.** Therefore the fourth apotome AB has been found. Q.E.F.

statement: To find the fifth apotome.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let A be a rational straight line set out, and let BG be a straight line commensurable in length with A; thus BG is rational [D10.1.3].

**Step 2.** Let two numbers DF and FE (treating these as numerical labels mn and np) be found such that neither has to the other the ratio of a square number to a square number. More precisely, let m and n be numbers such that m has not to n the ratio of a square number to a square number, and let p be a number such that m has not to p the ratio of a square number to a square number either, while n has not to p the ratio of a square number to a square number.

**Step 3.** As m is to n, so let the square on BG be to the square on GC, where GC is some straight line. Since the square on BG has to the square on GC the ratio which m has to n, the square on BG is commensurable with the square on GC [10.6]. Therefore the square on GC is rational, and GC is rational [D10.1.4].

**Step 4.** Since m has not to n the ratio of a square number to a square number, the square on BG has not to the square on GC the ratio of a square number to a square number. Therefore BG is incommensurable in length with GC [10.9]. Yet both are rational, so BG and GC are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; therefore BC, the remainder when we consider GC > BG or the difference appropriately, is an apotome [10.73].

**Step 5.** Now since the square on BG is to the square on GC as m is to n, by conversion of the ratio (componendo/dividendo reasoning on the squares), the square on GC exceeds the square on BG by some area. Let the square on GC be greater than the square on BG by the square on a straight line H. Then since sq(GC) : sq(BG) = m : n, we have sq(GC) - sq(BG) : sq(BG) = (m - n) : n.

**Step 6.** Now let it be arranged that as m is to p, so is the square on GC to the square on some line K. Since m has not to p the ratio of a square number to a square number, GC is incommensurable in length with K [10.9]. Let the square on GC exceed the square on BG by the square on H. We need to verify that H is incommensurable with GC. Since sq(GC) : sq(BG) = m : n, and sq(GC) : sq(K) = m : p, by 10.18 (taking the greater line GC, applying a parallelogram equal to the fourth of the square on BG, deficient by a square, and since it divides into parts that are incommensurable), the square on GC is greater than the square on BG by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with GC.

**Step 7.** I say that GC - BG (that is, the apotome with whole GC and annex BG) is a fifth apotome. We verify the conditions from the definition [D10.3.5]:
(a) GC and BG are rational and commensurable in square only, so their difference is an apotome [10.73].
(b) The square on the whole GC is greater than the square on the annex BG by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with the whole GC [Step 6].
(c) The annex BG is commensurable in length with the rational straight line A set out [Step 1].

**Step 8.** Since BG is commensurable in length with A but GC is incommensurable in length with BG [Step 4], then GC is incommensurable in length with A [10.13]. So the whole GC is not commensurable in length with A, while the annex BG is commensurable in length with A.

**Step 9.** Therefore, by the definition of the fifth apotome [D10.3.5], the line GC - BG (i.e., the apotome formed by subtracting BG from GC) is a fifth apotome. Thus the fifth apotome has been found. Q.E.F.

statement: To find the sixth apotome.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let there be set out a rational straight line A, and let three numbers E, BC, and CD be given such that E does not have to BC, nor BC to CD, the ratio that a square number has to a square number. [This is possible since there are infinitely many such numbers.]

**Step 2.** Let it be contrived that as E is to BC, so is the square on A to the square on FG [by 10.6, since we can find FG such that this ratio holds]. Then the square on A is commensurable with the square on FG [by 10.6]. Since E does not have to BC the ratio of a square number to a square number, the square on A does not have to the square on FG the ratio of a square number to a square number, so A is incommensurable in length with FG [by 10.9]. Therefore FG is rational and incommensurable in length with A, so FG is irrational in the sense of being incommensurable in length with the assigned rational line A.

**Step 3.** Since BC does not have to CD the ratio of a square number to a square number, and as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH [again by 10.6, finding GH accordingly], the square on FG is incommensurable with the square on GH [by 10.9]. Therefore FG is incommensurable in square with GH. Now both FG and GH are rational (commensurable in square with A), so FG and GH are rational and commensurable in square only. Therefore FH = FG - GH is an apotome [by 10.73].

**Step 4.** I say that FH is a sixth apotome. Since as E is to BC, so is the square on A to the square on FG, and as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH, therefore ex aequali, as E is to CD, so is the square on A to the square on GH [by 5.22]. But E does not have to CD the ratio of a square number to a square number (since E does not have to BC, nor BC to CD, the ratio of a square number to a square number, and neither does the product of such non-square ratios yield a square ratio). Therefore the square on A does not have to the square on GH the ratio of a square number to a square number, so A is incommensurable in length with GH [by 10.9].

**Step 5.** Therefore neither FG nor GH is commensurable in length with the rational straight line A. This satisfies one condition for a sixth apotome [by D10.3.6].

**Step 6.** Now I must show that the square on FG is greater than the square on GH by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with FG. Since as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH, therefore by conversion of ratio, as BC is to BD, so is the square on FG to the difference of the squares on FG and GH [by 5.19 with CN3], that is, to the square on the straight line K where the square on FG exceeds the square on GH by the square on K.

**Step 7.** We need BC not to have to BD the ratio of a square number to a square number. Since E, BC, CD were chosen so that BC does not have to CD the ratio of a square number to a square number, it follows that BC does not have to BD the ratio of a square number to a square number either [for if BC had to BD the ratio of a square number to a square number, then by 7.19 and the properties of numbers, BC would have to CD the ratio of a square number to a square number, contradicting our hypothesis].

**Step 8.** Therefore the square on FG does not have to the square on K the ratio of a square number to a square number, so FG is incommensurable in length with K [by 10.9]. Thus the square on FG is greater than the square on GH by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with FG.

**Step 9.** We have established: (i) FG and GH are rational and commensurable in square only, so FH is an apotome [by 10.73]; (ii) neither FG nor GH is commensurable in length with the rational straight line A; (iii) the square on FG is greater than the square on GH by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with FG. By definition D10.3.6, FH is a sixth apotome.

**Step 10.** Therefore the sixth apotome FH has been found. Q.E.F.

statement: If an area be contained by a rational straight line and a first apotome, the âsideâ of the area is an apotome.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let the area be contained by the rational straight line AC and the first apotome AD. I say that the "side" of the area AC * AD is an apotome.

**Step 2.** Since AD is a first apotome, let DG be the annex to AD, so that AG and GD are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, the square on AG is greater than the square on GD by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with AG, and AG is commensurable in length with the rational straight line AC set out [D10.3.1].

**Step 3.** Bisect DG at the point E [1.10], and to AG apply a parallelogram equal to the square on EG and deficient by a square figure; let this be the rectangle AF by FG [6.28]. Then, since the square on AG is greater than the square on GD by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with AG, and to the whole AG there has been applied the rectangle AF by FG equal to the fourth part of the square on DG (since EG is half of DG) and deficient by a square figure, therefore AF is commensurable in length with FG [10.17].

**Step 4.** Since AG is commensurable in length with AC, the whole AG is rational and commensurable in length with the rational straight line AC. Therefore the rectangle AC by AG is rational [10.19]. But AG equals AF + FG, and AF is commensurable in length with FG [Step 3].

**Step 5.** Now since AF is commensurable in length with FG, and AG is commensurable in length with each of AF and FG [10.15], and AG is commensurable in length with AC, therefore each of AF and FG is also commensurable in length with AC [10.12]. Hence each of AF and FG is rational and commensurable in length with AC.

**Step 6.** Therefore the rectangles AC by AF and AC by FG are each rational [10.19].

**Step 7.** Now, since DG is bisected at E, and the rectangle AF by FG equals the square on EG [Step 3 construction], we have by [2.5] that the rectangle AF by FG together with the square on AG minus the mean (i.e., the square on EG) relates to the segments. More precisely, since AF * FG = EG^2 and DG = 2*EG, we have AF * FG = (DG/2)^2 = DG^2/4.

**Step 8.** Let the square on H be made equal to the rectangle AC by AF, and the square on K be made equal to the rectangle AC by FG. Then the squares on H and K together equal AC * AF + AC * FG = AC * AG (since AF + FG = AG). That is, the squares on H and K together equal the rectangle AC by AG, which is rational [Step 5, 10.19]. So the sum of the squares on H and K is rational.

**Step 9.** Since AC * AF = H^2 and AC * FG = K^2, and these are both rational areas [Step 6], H and K are each rational straight lines [D10.1.4].

**Step 10.** Now consider the rectangle H by K. We have (H * K)^2 = H^2 * K^2 = (AC * AF)(AC * FG) = AC^2 * AF * FG. Also, AF * FG = EG^2 = DG^2/4 [Step 7]. Therefore (H * K)^2 = AC^2 * DG^2/4 = (AC * DG/2)^2, so H * K = AC * DG/2, meaning 2 * H * K = AC * DG.

**Step 11.** Now the rectangle AC by DG: since GD is the annex to the first apotome, GD is rational but incommensurable in length with AC (for if GD were commensurable in length with AC, then since AG is also commensurable in length with AC, AG and GD would be commensurable in length with each other [10.12], contradicting that they are commensurable in square only). Therefore AC and GD are rational and commensurable in square only, so the rectangle AC by GD is medial [10.21].

**Step 12.** Since 2 * H * K = AC * DG [Step 10], twice the rectangle contained by H and K is medial. Therefore the rectangle H by K is medial [Step 11]. But the sum of the squares on H and K is rational [Step 8].

**Step 13.** Now I must show that H and K are incommensurable in square. Since AC * AF = H^2 and AC * FG = K^2, we have H^2 : K^2 = AF : FG [6.1]. Since AF and FG are commensurable in length [Step 3], AF : FG is a ratio of number to number [10.5], so H^2 : K^2 is a ratio of number to number, meaning H and K are commensurable in square [10.9]. But then H and K are rational and commensurable in square. We must determine whether they are commensurable in length or in square only.

**Step 14.** Since H^2 : K^2 = AF : FG, and AF is commensurable in length with FG, H is commensurable in square with K. Now AF and FG are commensurable in length, so AF : FG is rational. But H^2 = AC * AF and K^2 = AC * FG, so H^2 : K^2 = AF : FG. For H and K to be commensurable in length, we would need H : K to be a ratio of number to number, i.e., AF : FG to be a ratio of a square number to a square number [10.9]. But there is no reason this must hold in general; AF and FG being commensurable in length means their ratio is of number to number, but not necessarily of square to square.

**Step 15.** Let me reconsider the construction more carefully. The area to be "sided" is AC * AD, where AD = AG - GD (the apotome). So the area equals AC * AG - AC * GD. We have AC * AG = H^2 + K^2 [Step 8] and AC * GD = 2*H*K [Step 10]. Therefore AC * AD = H^2 + K^2 - 2*H*K = (H - K)^2 [2.7, since H > K as AF > FG]. Thus the "side" of the area AC * AD is H - K.

**Step 16.** Now H and K are rational straight lines [Step 9]. We need to show H - K is an apotome, i.e., that H and K are commensurable in square only [10.73].

**Step 17.** Suppose for contradiction that H and K are commensurable in length. Then H^2 + K^2 and H * K are commensurable [by 10.15 applied to the commensurability of H^2 with K^2 when H is commensurable in length with K]. But H^2 + K^2 is rational [Step 8] and H * K is medial [Step 12], which means a rational area would be commensurable with a medial area, contradicting the fact that rational and medial areas are incommensurable [10.26, since a rational area cannot be commensurable with a medial area -- indeed, if H^2 + K^2 were commensurable with H*K, then since H^2 + K^2 is rational, H*K would also be rational by 10.12 applied to areas, contradicting that H*K is medial].

**Step 18.** More precisely: if H and K are commensurable in length, then H^2 is commensurable with H*K (since H^2 : H*K = H : K, a ratio of number to number, hence commensurable by 10.6). Similarly K^2 is commensurable with H*K. Therefore H^2 + K^2 is commensurable with H*K [10.15, 10.12]. But H^2 + K^2 is rational and 2*H*K is medial. Since H^2 + K^2 is commensurable with H*K, and 2*H*K is commensurable with H*K (differing by a factor of 2), H^2 + K^2 would be commensurable with 2*H*K. A rational area commensurable with a medial area is impossible, for a medial area is by definition irrational [D10.1.4, 10.21], while a rational area is rational. Two areas that are commensurable are either both rational or both irrational [by the nature of commensurability with the assigned rational square]. This is a contradiction.

**Step 19.** Therefore H and K are not commensurable in length. Since H and K are rational straight lines (commensurable in square with the assigned rational line), and they are not commensurable in length, they are commensurable in square only.

**Step 20.** Since H and K are rational and commensurable in square only, H - K is an apotome [10.73].

**Step 21.** And (H - K)^2 = AC * AD [Step 15], so the "side" of the area contained by the rational straight line AC and the first apotome AD is H - K, which is an apotome. Q.E.D.

statement: If an area be contained by a rational straight line and a second apotome, the âsideâ of the area is a first apotome of a medial straight line.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let the area be contained by the rational straight line AC and the second apotome AD. I say that the "side" of the area AC·AD is a first apotome of a medial straight line. Let DG be the annex to AD; then AG is the whole of the second apotome. By the definition of a second apotome (D10.3.2), DG is commensurable in length with the rational straight line set out, sq(AG) is greater than sq(DG) by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with AG, and AG is incommensurable in length with the assigned rational straight line. Since AC is rational and AD is a second apotome, let us proceed to find the "side" of the rectangle AC·AD.

**Step 2.** Let DG be the annex to AD, so that AG is the whole. By D10.3.2 the annex DG is commensurable in length with the rational straight line AC (since AC is rational and serves as the assigned rational line), while AG is incommensurable in length with AC. Also sq(AG) > sq(DG) by the square on a line commensurable in length with AG.

**Step 3.** Apply the rectangle AC·AG to AC, producing the breadth AG as width; similarly AC·DG to AC producing DG as width. The rectangle AC·AD equals the rectangle AC·AG minus the rectangle AC·DG (since AD = AG - DG). Since DG is commensurable in length with AC, and both are rational, the rectangle AC·DG is rational (by 10.19). Since AG is incommensurable in length with AC, and both are rational (commensurable in square with AC), the rectangle AC·AG is medial (by 10.21).

**Step 4.** Bisect DG at E, and to AG apply a rectangle equal to the square on EG and deficient by a square figure; let this rectangle be the rectangle AH·HG. Since sq(AG) > sq(DG) by the square on a line commensurable with AG (by the definition of second apotome), and the rectangle applied equals sq(EG) = (1/4)sq(DG), by 10.17 the segments AH and HG are commensurable in length.

**Step 5.** Describe a semicircle on AG with diameter AG, draw HK perpendicular to AG at H meeting the semicircle at K, and join AK, GK. Since the angle AKG is in a semicircle, the angle AKG is right (by 3.31). Since AH and HG are commensurable in length (Step 4), by 6.17 the rectangle AH·HG equals sq(KH), and by the relation sq(AK) = AH·AG and sq(GK) = GH·GA (from the right triangle and 6.8, or equivalently 2.14 and the properties of the semicircle), the squares on AK and GK can be analyzed.

**Step 6.** From the right triangle AKG with altitude KH, we have sq(AK) = AH·AG and sq(GK) = HG·GA (by 6.8 and the perpendicular from K to the diameter). Now AH is commensurable in length with HG (Step 4), so sq(AK) : sq(GK) = AH : HG (by 6.1), and therefore sq(AK) is commensurable with sq(GK). Thus AK is commensurable with GK in square (by 10.11).

**Step 7.** Since sq(AK) + sq(GK) = sq(AG) (by 1.47, as angle AKG is right), and AG is rational and incommensurable in length with AC, sq(AG) is a rational area but incommensurable with sq(AC). Now sq(AK) + sq(GK) = sq(AG). Since AG is incommensurable in length with AC, and sq(AG) = sq(AK) + sq(GK), the sum sq(AK) + sq(GK) equals the square on AG, which is rational in the sense of being commensurable with the square on AG. However, AG is rational (commensurable in square with AC) but incommensurable in length with AC, so sq(AG) is medial with respect to AC. Therefore sq(AK) + sq(GK) is medial (by 10.23 and 10.15, since sq(AK) and sq(GK) are commensurable and their sum is medial).

**Step 8.** Now the rectangle AK·GK: since sq(AK) = AH·AG and sq(GK) = HG·AG, we have 2·rect(AK, GK) = 2·KH·AG (from the altitude relation, but more precisely: rect(AK, GK)^2 = sq(AK)·sq(GK) = AH·AG·HG·AG = AH·HG·sq(AG)). Instead, note that the rectangle AC·AD = AC·AG - AC·DG, and from the semicircle construction, rect(AC, AD) = sq(AK') where AK' is the "side" we seek. We use the identity: since DG = 2·EG, rect(AC, DG) = 2·rect(AC, EG). Also, rect(AH, HG) = sq(EG) (from the application in Step 4 and the bisection), so sq(KH) = rect(AH, HG) = sq(EG), hence KH = EG.

**Step 9.** More directly: the rectangle AC·AD is the area whose "side" we seek. Apply this rectangle to a line to form a square; let the side of that square be denoted w. Following the standard construction of 10.54-10.59 and 10.91, set the problem up as follows. We have already that rect(AC, AG) is medial (Step 3) and rect(AC, DG) is rational (Step 3). We need two lines whose squares sum to rect(AC, AG) and whose product rectangle equals (1/2)·rect(AC, DG).

**Step 10.** Produce the rectangle AC·AG to get a medial area, and take the rectangle AC·DG which is rational. On a line FG equal to AC, apply the area rect(AC, AG) as a square on some line, or rather, following the approach of 10.91 more closely: Let MN and NO be straight lines such that sq(MN) + sq(NO) = rect(AC, AG) and rect(MN, NO) = (1/2)·rect(AC, DG). Then sq(MN) + sq(NO) is medial and rect(MN, NO) is rational.

**Step 11.** Since sq(MN) + sq(NO) is medial (it equals rect(AC, AG), which is medial by Step 3), and 2·rect(MN, NO) is rational (it equals rect(AC, DG), which is rational by Step 3), and the medial area sq(MN) + sq(NO) is incommensurable with the rational area 2·rect(MN, NO) (since a medial area is incommensurable with a rational area, by the definitions D10.1.3 and D10.1.4), the conditions match those of 10.34 and 10.74.

**Step 12.** We verify that MN and NO are medial and commensurable in square only. Since AH and HG are commensurable in length (Step 4), and sq(MN) = rect(AC, AH) and sq(NO) = rect(AC, HG), where AC is rational, we need AH and HG to be rational. Since AG is rational (it is commensurable in square with AC) and AH, HG are parts of AG with AH commensurable with HG, but AG is incommensurable in length with AC. Now rect(AC, AH) and rect(AC, HG) are the squares on MN and NO respectively. Since AH is incommensurable in length with AC (because AG is incommensurable in length with AC, and AH is a part of AG commensurable with AG by 10.15), the rectangle AC·AH is medial (by 10.21). Thus sq(MN) is medial, so MN is medial (by D10.1.4). Similarly sq(NO) is medial, so NO is medial.

**Step 13.** Since sq(MN) = rect(AC, AH) and sq(NO) = rect(AC, HG), we have sq(MN) : sq(NO) = AH : HG (by 6.1). Since AH is commensurable with HG (Step 4), sq(MN) is commensurable with sq(NO) (by 10.6). Therefore MN is commensurable with NO in square. Since sq(MN) + sq(NO) is medial and 2·rect(MN, NO) is rational, MN and NO are incommensurable in square with each other only, not in length (if they were commensurable in length, then sq(MN) + sq(NO) would have a fixed ratio to rect(MN, NO), making the medial commensurable with the rational, which is impossible by 10.26). So MN and NO are commensurable in square only.

**Step 14.** Since MN and NO are medial straight lines commensurable in square only, and they contain a rational rectangle (rect(MN, NO) is rational), the difference MN - NO is a first apotome of a medial straight line (by 10.74, which defines the first apotome of a medial straight line as the remainder when from a medial straight line is subtracted a medial straight line commensurable in square only and containing with it a rational rectangle).

**Step 15.** It remains to show that MN - NO is indeed the "side" of the rectangle AC·AD. We have sq(MN) + sq(NO) = rect(AC, AG) and 2·rect(MN, NO) = rect(AC, DG). Then sq(MN) + sq(NO) - 2·rect(MN, NO) = rect(AC, AG) - rect(AC, DG) = rect(AC, AG - DG) = rect(AC, AD). But sq(MN) + sq(NO) - 2·rect(MN, NO) = sq(MN - NO) (by 2.7). Therefore sq(MN - NO) = rect(AC, AD), so MN - NO is the "side" of the area contained by AC and AD.

**Step 16.** Therefore the "side" of the area contained by the rational straight line AC and the second apotome AD is a first apotome of a medial straight line. Q.E.D.

statement: If an area be contained by a rational straight line and a third apotome, the âsideâ of the area is a second apotome of a medial straight line.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let the area AB be contained by the rational straight line AC and the third apotome AD. I say that the "side" of the area AB is a second apotome of a medial straight line.

**Step 2.** Let DG be the annex to AD, so that AG and GD are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, neither AG nor GD is commensurable in length with the rational straight line AC, and the square on AG is greater than the square on GD by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with AG. [D10.3.3]

**Step 3.** Apply to AC the square on AG, producing AH as breadth, and apply to AC the square on DG, producing KH as breadth. Since AG and DG are each incommensurable in length with AC, and AC is rational, the squares on AG and on DG are each incommensurable with the square on AC. But the square on AC is rational, so the squares on AG and on DG are each irrational, hence medial. [D10.1.3, D10.1.4] Therefore AH and KH, being the breadths produced when medial areas are applied to the rational straight line AC, are each rational and incommensurable in length with AC. [10.22]

**Step 4.** Since the square on AG is greater than the square on DG by the square on a straight line commensurable with AG, and AG and DG are commensurable in square only, by 10.17 if we apply to AG a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on DG and deficient by a square figure, it divides AG into parts commensurable in length.

**Step 5.** Since AG : DG :: sq(AG) : rect(AG, DG), and since sq(AG) = AC * AH and rect(AG, DG) is related to the applied areas, consider that sq(AG) - sq(DG) = AC * (AH - KH) = AC * LH (where L is such that the area corresponding to AH minus KH gives LH). Since the square on AG is greater than the square on DG by the square on a straight line commensurable with AG, by 10.14, the corresponding breadths maintain this commensurability relationship.

**Step 6.** Now the square on AG is commensurable with the square on DG, since AG and DG are commensurable in square. [D10.1.2] Therefore AH is commensurable with KH. [10.11, 6.1]

**Step 7.** But AH and KH are each rational and incommensurable in length with AC (Step 3). And AH is commensurable with KH. Therefore AH and KH are rational straight lines commensurable in square only (since they are commensurable — and being rational lines incommensurable with AC, their commensurability with each other makes them commensurable in length). In fact, since sq(AG) : sq(DG) :: AH : KH [6.1, 10.11], and AG, DG are commensurable in square (so sq(AG) is commensurable with sq(DG)), AH is commensurable in length with KH.

**Step 8.** Since AG and DG are commensurable in square only, AG is incommensurable in length with DG, so sq(AG) is incommensurable with rect(AG, DG). [6.1, 10.11] But sq(AG) = AC * AH, so AC * AH is incommensurable with rect(AG, DG).

**Step 9.** Now rect(AG, DG) is irrational since AG and DG are rational and commensurable in square only, so rect(AG, DG) is medial. [10.21] Apply twice rect(AG, DG) to AC; let the breadth be MH. Since rect(AG, DG) is medial and AC is rational, MH is rational and incommensurable in length with AC. [10.22]

**Step 10.** Since AD = AG - DG, we have sq(AD) = sq(AG) + sq(DG) - 2 * rect(AG, DG). [2.7] Therefore the area AB = AC * AD, and sq(AD) applied to AC gives AH + KH - MH (that is, the breadth for sq(AG) plus the breadth for sq(DG) minus the breadth for 2 * rect(AG, DG)). But we need the side of the rectangle AC * AD, not the square on AD.

**Step 11.** Let us restart the construction more carefully. Apply the rectangle AC * AD to AC. Since AD is a third apotome, let AD = AG - GD where AG, GD satisfy the conditions in D10.3.3. Let the square on a straight line w equal the area AC * AD, so that w is the "side" of the area. We wish to show w is a second apotome of a medial straight line.

**Step 12.** Following the method of 10.91 and 10.92, let BG be set equal to AG (extending the line) so that DG is the annex, and bisect GD at E. Apply to AG a rectangle equal to the square on EG and deficient by a square; let this give AG divided as the rectangle AO * OG = sq(EG), with O a suitable point. By 10.17, since sq(AG) exceeds sq(GD) by the square on a line commensurable with AG, the segments AO and OG are commensurable in length.

**Step 13.** Equivalently, apply the area AC * AD to the line AC. By 10.56 (which handles the third binomial and yields a second bimedial), the structure of the third apotome mirrors that. Following Euclid's method for apotome propositions: set out a rational straight line AC, and let the third apotome AD have annex DG, with AG the whole. Apply to AC the areas: let sq(AG) = AC * AH and sq(DG) = AC * KL, so AH and KL are the breadths.

**Step 14.** Since AG, DG are rational and commensurable in square only, and each is incommensurable in length with AC: the squares sq(AG) and sq(DG) are medial (as in Step 3). Hence AH and KL, being each a medial area divided by rational AC, are rational and incommensurable in length with AC. [10.22]

**Step 15.** Since sq(AG) is commensurable with sq(DG) (AG, DG being commensurable in square), AH is commensurable in length with KL. [6.1, 10.11] So AH, KL are rational and commensurable in length, hence AH - KL is rational. But both are incommensurable in length with AC.

**Step 16.** Now sq(AG) - sq(DG) = AC * (AH - KL). Since AD = AG - GD, we have rect(AG, DG) relates to the configuration. By 2.5, rect(AG, DG) + sq(GE) = sq(AE) where E bisects AD (note: E bisects the segment from G to... let us use 2.7 directly): sq(AG - GD) = sq(AG) + sq(GD) - 2*rect(AG, GD). So AC * AD is not sq(AD).

**Step 17.** We proceed directly. Let the area be S = AC * AD, and let w be a straight line such that sq(w) = S. We need to construct w explicitly. Following Euclid's approach in 10.91-10.92: bisect DG at E, and apply to AG a rectangle equal to sq(EG) falling short by a square figure. By 10.17, since sq(AG) > sq(DG) by the square on a line commensurable with AG, the resulting segments are commensurable. Let this application produce the point H on AG such that AH * HG = sq(EG).

**Step 18.** Then by 2.5, AH * HG + sq(EG) = sq(half of AG adjusted)... Instead, apply the standard Euclidean construction: since sq(AG) > sq(GD) by the square on a line commensurable with AG, and GD is bisected at E, apply to AG a parallelogram equal to sq(EG) and deficient by a square. This determines points on AG. The segments AH, HG are commensurable in length. [10.17]

**Step 19.** Set out that rect(AH, HG) = sq(EG). Since DG is bisected at E, by 2.5: rect(DG, GD) + sq(EG) is related, giving us sq(EG) = sq(GD/2). Actually, DG bisected at E means EG = DG/2 and DE = DG/2. Now we apply to AG a parallelogram equal to sq(EG) = sq(DG/2) = sq(DG)/4, deficient by a square. By 10.17, AH and HG are commensurable in length.

**Step 20.** Now construct: let AN = AH and let o be a point such that sq(o) = AC * AN, and let p be such that sq(p) = AC * HG. Then sq(o) + sq(p) = AC * (AN + HG) = AC * AG. Also, o and p are incommensurable in square (since AN and HG are commensurable in length, and the construction yields lines related to medial areas).

**Step 21.** Since AN * HG = sq(DG)/4 (from Step 19), we get AC * AN * AC * HG = sq(AC) * sq(DG)/4, so rect(sq(o), sq(p)) in area terms: sq(o) * sq(p) = sq(AC) * AN * HG = sq(AC) * sq(DG)/4. Hence o * p = (AC * DG)/2 (taking the positive root), and 2 * rect(o, p) = AC * DG.

**Step 22.** But rect(AG, DG) is medial (since AG, DG are rational commensurable in square only) [10.21]. Therefore AC * DG: since AC is rational and DG is rational but incommensurable in length with AC (given in the third apotome definition), AC * DG is medial [10.21, as AC and DG are rational but incommensurable in length]. Hence 2 * rect(o, p) = AC * DG is medial, so rect(o, p) is medial.

**Step 23.** Now sq(o) + sq(p) = AC * AG. Since AG is rational and incommensurable in length with AC, the rectangle AC * AG is medial [10.21]. So sq(o) + sq(p) is medial.

**Step 24.** We need to show that sq(o) + sq(p) is incommensurable with rect(o, p). We have sq(o) + sq(p) = AC * AG and 2 * rect(o, p) = AC * DG. So (sq(o) + sq(p)) : 2*rect(o, p) = AG : DG. [6.1] Since AG and DG are incommensurable in length, AG : DG is a ratio of incommensurable magnitudes, so sq(o) + sq(p) is incommensurable with 2*rect(o, p), hence with rect(o, p). [10.11]

**Step 25.** Now sq(o) = AC * AN and sq(p) = AC * HG. Since AN and HG are commensurable in length (Step 18), AC * AN is commensurable with AC * HG [6.1, 10.11], so sq(o) is commensurable with sq(p). Therefore o and p are commensurable in square. [D10.1.2]

**Step 26.** Since sq(o) + sq(p) is medial (Step 23), o and p are not commensurable in square with a rational line in the standard sense; in particular, o and p are medial straight lines. Since sq(o) = AC * AN, and AN is rational (as shown: AN is commensurable with AH which is rational [Step 14-15]), sq(o) is the rectangle of a rational line AC and a rational line AN with AN incommensurable in length with AC. So sq(o) is medial [10.21], hence o is medial. Similarly p is medial.

**Step 27.** We have established: o and p are medial straight lines, commensurable in square only (since they are commensurable in square by Step 25, and incommensurable in length because if they were commensurable in length, sq(o) + sq(p) and rect(o,p) would be commensurable, contradicting Step 24), their sum of squares is medial (Step 23), and the rectangle contained by them is medial (Step 22), and the sum of squares is incommensurable with the rectangle (Step 24).

**Step 28.** Now w = o - p (since AD = AG - GD, and the construction mirrors the subtraction). We have sq(w) = sq(o) + sq(p) - 2*rect(o, p) = AC * AG - AC * DG = AC * (AG - GD) = AC * AD, confirming that sq(w) equals the original area. [2.7]

**Step 29.** Since o and p are medial and commensurable in square only, and they contain with each other a medial rectangle (Step 22), the remainder o - p is a second apotome of a medial straight line. [10.75]

**Step 30.** Therefore the "side" of the area contained by the rational straight line AC and the third apotome AD is a second apotome of a medial straight line. Q.E.D.

statement: If an area be contained by a rational straight line and a fourth apotome, the âsideâ of the area is minor.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let the area be contained by the rational straight line A and the fourth apotome BG, and let BG be divided at H so that BH is the whole and HG the annex. By the definition of a fourth apotome (D10.3.4), BH is commensurable in length with the rational straight line A, the square on BH is greater than the square on HG by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with BH, and BH and HG are commensurable in square only.

**Step 2.** Since sq(BH) > sq(HG) by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with BH, by 10.18 (applied to BH and HG), if we apply to BH a parallelogram equal to one-fourth of sq(HG) and deficient by a square figure, it divides BH into parts that are incommensurable in length.

**Step 3.** Bisect BH at E, so that BE = EH. Apply to BH a rectangle equal to one-fourth of sq(HG) and deficient by a square, producing segments BF and FH (where F lies between B and H). By Step 2, BF and FH are incommensurable in length. Since BH is bisected at E and divided unequally at F, by 2.5, the rectangle BF . FH together with sq(EF) equals sq(EH). But the rectangle BF . FH equals one-fourth of sq(HG), so sq(EH) = (1/4) sq(HG) + sq(EF), whence sq(EH) - sq(EF) = (1/4) sq(HG). Since BH = 2 EH and HG = 2 times the side whose square is (1/4) sq(HG), this yields sq(BH) - sq(HG) = 4 sq(EF), i.e., sq(BH) = sq(HG) + 4 sq(EF). Equivalently, sq(EH) > sq(EF).

**Step 4.** Since BH is commensurable in length with A (both rational), and BH = 2 EH, the line EH is also commensurable in length with A (for halving a rational line yields a rational line commensurable with A, by 10.15 and 10.12). Thus sq(EH) is commensurable with sq(A), i.e., sq(EH) is a rational area.

**Step 5.** Since BF and FH are incommensurable in length, BH (= BF + FH) is incommensurable in length with each of BF and FH by 10.16. But BH is rational and commensurable with A in length, so BF is incommensurable in length with A. The rectangle A . BF is therefore irrational, and the square equal to it (i.e., the square on a straight line we call s1) is irrational. Hence s1 is irrational.

**Step 6.** Similarly, since FH is incommensurable in length with BH and hence with A, the rectangle A . FH is irrational. The straight line s2, whose square equals the rectangle A . FH, is likewise irrational.

**Step 7.** Since BF is incommensurable in length with FH, by 10.11 the rectangle A . BF is incommensurable with the rectangle A . FH, i.e., sq(s1) is incommensurable with sq(s2). Therefore s1 and s2 are incommensurable in square.

**Step 8.** Now the total area A . BG = A . BH - A . HG (by 1.43 or the distributive property from 2.1 applied to the difference). Since BH and HG are rational and commensurable in square only, the rectangle BH . HG is irrational (by 10.21, since they are commensurable in square only and rational). The rectangle A . BH is rational (since A and BH are both rational and commensurable in length, by 10.19). Also, A . BG = A . BF - A . FG + (A . FH - ...). More precisely, the total area A . BG can be decomposed as follows.

**Step 9.** Consider the rectangle A . BH. By 2.5, since BH is bisected at E and cut at F, the rectangle BF . FH + sq(EF) = sq(EH), so BF . FH = sq(EH) - sq(EF). We set up lines so that sq(s1) = A . BF and sq(s2) = A . FH.

**Step 10.** We need to show sq(s1) + sq(s2) is rational and 2 rect(s1, s2) is medial. Now sq(s1) + sq(s2) = A . BF + A . FH = A . (BF + FH) = A . BH. Since both A and BH are rational and commensurable in length, A . BH is rational by 10.19. Hence sq(s1) + sq(s2) is rational.

**Step 11.** Next, consider 2 rect(s1, s2). We have sq(s1) . sq(s2) = (A . BF)(A . FH) = sq(A) . (BF . FH). But BF . FH = (1/4) sq(HG) by construction. So sq(s1) . sq(s2) = sq(A) . (1/4) sq(HG), meaning rect(s1, s2) = (1/2) A . HG (by 6.17 and properties of proportions). Thus 2 rect(s1, s2) = A . HG.

**Step 12.** We must show A . HG is medial. Since BH is commensurable in length with A, and HG is commensurable in square only with BH (by the definition of the fourth apotome), HG is commensurable in square only with A (by 10.13 and 10.12 — specifically, HG is incommensurable in length with BH and hence with A, but the square on HG is commensurable with the square on BH and hence rational). Therefore HG is rational (its square is rational) but incommensurable in length with A. By 10.21, the rectangle A . HG is irrational, and the square equal to it is irrational — the side of that square is medial. Hence A . HG is a medial area. Therefore 2 rect(s1, s2) is medial.

**Step 13.** Further, we show that sq(s1) + sq(s2) is incommensurable with 2 rect(s1, s2). We have sq(s1) + sq(s2) = A . BH and 2 rect(s1, s2) = A . HG. The ratio of A . BH to A . HG equals BH : HG (by 6.1). Since BH and HG are commensurable in square only, they are incommensurable in length, so the ratio BH : HG is not a ratio of number to number (by 10.7). Therefore A . BH is incommensurable with A . HG by 10.11, i.e., sq(s1) + sq(s2) is incommensurable with 2 rect(s1, s2).

**Step 14.** Now the "side" of the area A . BG is s1 - s2 (where s1 > s2, since BF > FH follows from the construction). We have established: s1 and s2 are incommensurable in square (Step 7); sq(s1) + sq(s2) is rational (Step 10); 2 rect(s1, s2) is medial (Step 12). By 10.76, the straight line s1 - s2 is the irrational line called minor.

**Step 15.** Therefore, if an area be contained by a rational straight line and a fourth apotome, the "side" of the area is minor. Q.E.D.

statement: If an area be contained by a rational straight line and a fifth apotome, the âsideâ of the area is a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let the area AB be contained by the rational straight line rho and the fifth apotome AD. Let DG be the annex to AD, so that AG is the whole of the apotome and AD = AG - GD. I say that the "side" of the area AB is a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole.

**Step 2.** By the definition of a fifth apotome (D10.3.5), the annex GD is commensurable in length with rho, the whole AG is incommensurable in length with rho, and the square on AG is greater than the square on GD by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with AG. Since AD is an apotome, AG and GD are rational straight lines commensurable in square only [by 10.73].

**Step 3.** Bisect GD at E [by 1.10]. Apply to AG a rectangle equal to the square on EG and deficient by a square figure [by 6.28]; let the resulting parts of AG be AH and HG, so that AH + HG = AG and AH * HG = EG^2 = (GD/2)^2.

**Step 4.** Since the square on AG exceeds the square on GD by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with AG (D10.3.5), and the rectangle equal to the fourth part of the square on GD has been applied to AG deficient by a square, it follows by 10.18 that AH is incommensurable in length with HG.

**Step 5.** Construct straight lines MN and NO such that the square on MN equals the rectangle rho by AH, and the square on NO equals the rectangle rho by HG, with MN > NO [by 2.14 and P1].

**Step 6.** Then the sum of the squares on MN and NO equals rho * AH + rho * HG = rho * (AH + HG) = rho * AG [by 2.1].

**Step 7.** Now compute 2 * MN * NO. We have (2 * MN * NO)^2 = 4 * (sq(MN)) * (sq(NO)) = 4 * (rho * AH) * (rho * HG) = 4 * rho^2 * (AH * HG). Since AH * HG = EG^2 = (GD/2)^2, we get 4 * rho^2 * (GD/2)^2 = rho^2 * GD^2. Therefore 2 * MN * NO = rho * GD.

**Step 8.** Consider sq(MN) - sq(NO) = rho * AH - rho * HG = rho * (AH - HG). Then sq(MN - NO) = sq(MN) + sq(NO) - 2 * MN * NO = rho * AG - rho * GD = rho * (AG - GD) = rho * AD = the area AB. Therefore MN - NO is the "side" of the area AB.

**Step 9.** We now verify that MN - NO satisfies the conditions of Proposition 10.77, which defines "that which produces with a rational area a medial whole." Three conditions must hold: (i) MN and NO are incommensurable in square, (ii) the sum sq(MN) + sq(NO) is medial, and (iii) twice the rectangle MN by NO is rational.

**Step 10.** Verification of (iii): By Step 7, 2 * MN * NO = rho * GD. Since GD is commensurable in length with rho (D10.3.5), and both are rational, the rectangle rho * GD is rational [by 10.19]. Therefore twice the rectangle MN by NO is rational.

**Step 11.** Verification of (ii): By Step 6, sq(MN) + sq(NO) = rho * AG. Since AG is rational and rho is rational, but AG is incommensurable in length with rho (D10.3.5), AG and rho are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. Therefore the rectangle rho * AG is medial [by 10.21]. So the sum of the squares on MN, NO is medial.

**Step 12.** Verification of (i): Since AH is incommensurable in length with HG (Step 4), the rectangle rho * AH is incommensurable with the rectangle rho * HG [by 6.1 and 10.11]. That is, sq(MN) is incommensurable with sq(NO). Therefore MN is incommensurable in square with NO.

**Step 13.** Since MN and NO are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on them is medial, and twice the rectangle contained by them is rational, MN - NO is that which produces with a rational area a medial whole [by 10.77].

**Step 14.** But MN - NO is the "side" of the area AB (Step 8). Therefore, if an area be contained by a rational straight line and a fifth apotome, the "side" of the area is a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole. Q.E.D.

statement: If an area be contained by a rational straight line and a sixth apotome, the âsideâ of the area is a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole.
proof:
**Step 1.** Let the area AB be contained by the rational straight line AC and the sixth apotome AD. I say that the "side" of the area AB is a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole.

**Step 2.** Since AD is a sixth apotome, let DG be the annex to AD, so that AG is the whole and GD is the annex. By the definition of a sixth apotome (D10.3.6), AG and GD are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, neither AG nor GD is commensurable in length with the rational straight line AC set out, and the square on AG is greater than the square on GD by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with AG.

**Step 3.** Since the square on AG is greater than the square on GD by the square on a straight line incommensurable with AG, if there be applied to AG a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on GD and deficient by a square figure, it will divide AG into parts which are incommensurable in length [10.18].

**Step 4.** Let DG be bisected at the point E, let there be applied to AG a parallelogram equal to the square on EG and deficient by a square figure, and let it be the rectangle AF by FG. Then AF is incommensurable in length with FG [10.18].

**Step 5.** Now since AG is incommensurable in length with AC, both AG and GD being incommensurable in length with AC, and since AG and GD are rational, the rectangle contained by AC and AG is medial, and likewise the rectangle contained by AC and DG is medial [10.21].

**Step 6.** Apply to AC the rectangle AH equal to the square on AG, producing AH as breadth, and apply to AC the rectangle GK equal to the square on GD, producing GK as breadth. Then since the square on AG is incommensurable with the square on GD (for AG and GD are commensurable in square only, hence their squares are commensurable, but AG is incommensurable in length with GD, and since each is rational, the rectangle AG by GD is irrational; however, we note that since AG and GD are rational and commensurable in square only, the squares on AG and on GD are each rational areas), and these squares are applied to the rational line AC, the breadths AH and GK are each rational and incommensurable in length with AC [10.22].

**Step 7.** Since AF is incommensurable in length with FG, the square on AF is incommensurable with the rectangle AF by FG [10.11]. But the square on AG is commensurable with the square on AF, since AG is commensurable in square with AF (they are both derived from the same partition); and the rectangle AG by GD is commensurable with the rectangle AF by FG, since AG by GD equals twice AF by FG by the properties of the bisection and the application [2.5]. Therefore the square on AG is incommensurable with the rectangle AG by GD [10.13].

**Step 8.** But the square on AG equals AH (as applied to AC), and the rectangle AG by GD, taken twice, equals the area by which AH exceeds GK applied to AC. Thus AH is incommensurable with the rectangle contained by AG and GD applied to AC. Hence the breadth corresponding to AH is incommensurable in length with the breadth corresponding to twice the rectangle AG by GD, both being applied to the rational line AC [10.11].

**Step 9.** Now since the rectangle AC by AG is medial [Step 5], the area AH (the square on AG applied to AC) has AH as breadth, and this area is rational (square on a rational line), making the breadth rational but incommensurable in length with AC [10.22]. Similarly for GK.

**Step 10.** Since AG by GD equals the rectangle contained by AG and GD, and twice this rectangle applied to AC gives the difference of areas corresponding to the decomposition, and since AG and GD are commensurable in square only with neither commensurable in length with AC, twice the rectangle AG by GD is medial [10.21], applied to the rational line AC, gives a breadth which is rational and incommensurable in length with AC.

**Step 11.** Moreover, AH is incommensurable with GK applied in this way [from Step 8], so the breadths are incommensurable in length, and AH and GK are both medial areas. Further, since AF is incommensurable in length with FG, and the areas corresponding to the squares on AF and on FG (applied to AC) produce the sum of squares which is medial, and twice the rectangle AF by FG applied to AC is also medial, and these two are incommensurable with each other [from Steps 7-8].

**Step 12.** Let the square on MN equal the rectangle AC by AF (i.e., the area corresponding to AF), and let the square on NO equal the rectangle AC by FG, with MN and NO laid along the same straight line. Then the rectangle MN by NO is equal to half of the rectangle AC by AG times the appropriate factor, and in particular MO is a straight line such that MN and NO are incommensurable in square [10.11, from AF incommensurable with FG applied through 10.22].

**Step 13.** The sum of the squares on MN and on NO equals the rectangle AC by AG (since AF + FG = AG, the rectangles AC by AF and AC by FG sum to AC by AG), which is a medial area [Step 5, since AG is incommensurable in length with AC and both are rational, giving a medial rectangle by 10.21].

**Step 14.** Twice the rectangle MN by NO equals the rectangle AC by DG. This is because AG by GD = 2(AF by FG) from the bisection at E and the application [2.5], and the rectangle AC by GD = AC times GD, which relates to twice the rectangle of the parts. Since GD is incommensurable in length with AC and both are rational, AC by GD is medial [10.21].

**Step 15.** Since the square on AG is incommensurable with the rectangle AG by GD [Step 7], and the square on AG corresponds to the sum of squares on MN and NO (as AC by AG), while the rectangle AG by GD corresponds to twice the rectangle MN by NO (as AC by GD), the sum of the squares on MN and NO is incommensurable with twice the rectangle MN by NO.

**Step 16.** Therefore MN and NO are two straight lines incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on them is medial [Step 13], twice the rectangle contained by them is medial [Step 14], and the sum of the squares on them is incommensurable with twice the rectangle contained by them [Step 15].

**Step 17.** Therefore MO = MN + NO is the side of the sum of two medial areas [10.41]. Now MN - NO (or NO subtracted from MN, taking whichever is greater) gives a straight line whose square equals the area AB. More precisely, the square on the whole line MO corresponds to AC by AD plus 2(rect MN by NO), while we need the "side" of the area AC by AD. Since AD = AG - GD, the rectangle AC by AD = AC by AG - AC by GD = (sq on MN + sq on NO) - 2(rect MN by NO) = sq on (MN - NO), taking the appropriate difference.

**Step 18.** Therefore the "side" of the area AB is MN - NO (the remainder when the lesser is subtracted from the greater). Since MN and NO are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on them is medial, twice the rectangle contained by them is medial, and the squares on them are incommensurable with twice the rectangle, MN - NO is the straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole [10.78].

**Step 19.** Therefore, if an area be contained by a rational straight line and a sixth apotome, the "side" of the area is a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole. Q.E.D.

statement: The square on an apotome applied to a rational straight line produces as breadth a first apotome.
proof:
